story-7151abe6e9567f8e0233eea3.content: CHINESE MANUFACTURERS: Saudi sovereign wealth will not pay a private importer’s overdue invoice. There is a dangerous assumption in international trade: if a country is rich, its companies must be financially safe. Saudi Arabia demonstrates why that assumption can be costly. The Kingdom’s public debt reached SAR 1.774 trillion ($473 billion) by the end of September 2026, up from SAR 1.519 trillion at the beginning of the year. Its budget deficit reached SAR 244.3 billion in just nine months. These figures do not prove that Saudi importers are defaulting. But they raise important questions about financial pressure throughout an economy heavily influenced by public spending. Saudi companies importing machinery, electronics, construction materials and consumer products may depend on payments from contractors, retailers or government-linked projects. If those payments are delayed, foreign suppliers offering unsecured credit can become exposed. The US International Trade Administration explicitly warns exporters to protect themselves against late payment and non-payment in Saudi Arabia. This warning should not be ignored. A commercial registration is not a payment guarantee. A luxury office is not proof of liquidity. A government contract is not necessarily cash in the bank. For factories selling on 60, 90 or 180-day credit, the customer’s actual cash flow matters more than the country’s reputation. story-7239d2331b2e024e187a6b58.content:
Last week, I spoke with two US Marines who spent much of last year deployed in the Pacific, conducting training exercises from South Korea to the Philippines. Both were responsible for analyzing surveillance to warn their superiors about possible threats to the unit. But this deployment was unique: For the first time, they were using generative AI to scour intelligence, through a chatbot interface similar to ChatGPT. 

As I wrote in my new story, this experiment is the latest evidence of the Pentagon’s push to use generative AI—tools that can engage in humanlike conversation—throughout its ranks, for tasks including surveillance. Consider this phase two of the US military’s AI push, where phase one began back in 2017 with older types of AI, like computer vision to analyze drone imagery. Though this newest phase began under the Biden administration, there’s fresh urgency as Elon Musk’s DOGE and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth push loudly for AI-fueled efficiency. 

As I also write in my story, this push raises alarms from some AI safety experts about whether large language models are fit to analyze subtle pieces of intelligence in situations with high geopolitical stakes. It also accelerates the US toward a world where AI is not just analyzing military data but suggesting actions—for example, generating lists of targets. Proponents say this promises greater accuracy and fewer civilian deaths, but many human rights groups argue the opposite. 

With that in mind, here are three open questions to keep your eye on as the US military, and others around the world, bring generative AI to more parts of the so-called “kill chain.”

What are the limits of “human in the loop”?

Talk to as many defense-tech companies as I have and you’ll hear one phrase repeated quite often: “human in the loop.” It means that the AI is responsible for particular tasks, and humans are there to check its work. It’s meant to be a safeguard against the most dismal scenarios—AI wrongfully ordering a deadly strike, for example—but also against more trivial mishaps. Implicit in this idea is an admission that AI will make mistakes, and a promise that humans will catch them.

But the complexity of AI systems, which pull from thousands of pieces of data, make that a herculean task for humans, says Heidy Khlaaf, who is chief AI scientist at the AI Now Institute, a research organization, and previously led safety audits for AI-powered systems.

“‘Human in the loop’ is not always a meaningful mitigation,” she says. When an AI model relies on thousands of data points to draw conclusions, “it wouldn’t really be possible for a human to sift through that amount of information to determine if the AI output was erroneous.” As AI systems rely on more and more data, this problem scales up.

Is AI making it easier or harder to know what should be classified?

In the Cold War era of US military intelligence, information was captured through covert means, written up into reports by experts in Washington, and then stamped “Top Secret,” with access restricted to those with proper clearances. The age of big data, and now the advent of generative AI to analyze that data, is upending the old paradigm in lots of ways.

One specific problem is called classification by compilation. Imagine that hundreds of unclassified documents all contain separate details of a military system. Someone who managed to piece those together could reveal important information that on its own would be classified. For years, it was reasonable to assume that no human could connect the dots, but this is exactly the sort of thing that large language models excel at. 

With the mountain of data growing each day, and then AI constantly creating new analyses, “I don’t think anyone’s come up with great answers for what the appropriate classification of all these products should be,” says Chris Mouton, a senior engineer for RAND, who recently tested how well suited generative AI is for intelligence and analysis. Underclassifying is a US security concern, but lawmakers have also criticized the Pentagon for overclassifying information. 

The defense giant Palantir is positioning itself to help, by offering its AI tools to determine whether a piece of data should be classified or not. It’s also working with Microsoft on AI models that would train on classified data. 

How high up the decision chain should AI go?

Zooming out for a moment, it’s worth noting that the US military’s adoption of AI has in many ways followed consumer patterns. Back in 2017, when apps on our phones were getting good at recognizing our friends in photos, the Pentagon launched its own computer vision effort, called Project Maven, to analyze drone footage and identify targets.

Now, as large language models enter our work and personal lives through interfaces such as ChatGPT, the Pentagon is tapping some of these models to analyze surveillance. 

So what’s next? For consumers, it’s agentic AI, or models that can not just converse with you and analyze information but go out onto the internet and perform actions on your behalf. It’s also personalized AI, or models that learn from your private data to be more helpful. 

All signs point to the prospect that military AI models will follow this trajectory as well. A report published in March from Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology found a surge in military adoption of AI to assist in decision-making. “Military commanders are interested in AI’s potential to improve decision-making, especially at the operational level of war,” the authors wrote.

In October, the Biden administration released its national security memorandum on AI, which provided some safeguards for these scenarios. This memo hasn’t been formally repealed by the Trump administration, but President Trump has indicated that the race for competitive AI in the US needs more innovation and less oversight. Regardless, it’s clear that AI is quickly moving up the chain not just to handle administrative grunt work, but to assist in the most high-stakes, time-sensitive decisions. 

I’ll be following these three questions closely. If you have information on how the Pentagon might be handling these questions, please reach out via Signal at jamesodonnell.22.

story-746571609cba279614fe78a4.content: The Global Outage Mea Culpa: Why Enterprise Cloud Trust Is Officially Broken A stage apology and an admission of having work to do do not qualify as an explanation, especially not when global commerce just took a direct hit. Satya Nadella addressed last week's catastrophic Outlook blackout at Ignite by framing digital infrastructure as the dial tone for the world, before quickly steering the conversation right back to Copilot and the next cycle of product announcements. https://t.co/tTVRmouzM3 The enterprise cannot simply shrug this off and proceed as normal. Over the past week, I have been talking directly with enterprise leaders whose critical operations ground to a complete standstill. Across my client base alone, the financial fallout from operational paralysis, stranded transactions, and lost productivity easily exceeds 1 billion USD. For these organizations, trust has evaporated. They are no longer having hypothetical strategy sessions; they are actively discussing an exodus from their Microsoft infrastructure to protect their businesses from catastrophic vendor concentration risk. From an engineering perspective, there is zero excuse for this failure mode. You do not design and operate a tier-one global cloud architecture where a single deployment mistake or routing flaw can propagate unrestricted across international boundaries and knock out services in dozens of countries simultaneously. Fundamental distributed systems architecture requires rigid blast-radius containment, decoupled fault domains, and autonomous regional isolation. If an operational issue can still cascade globally through automated traffic management and bring down key gateway tiers worldwide, it points to systemic failure. Either the underlying architecture is abysmal, the operational and deployment controls are fundamentally broken, or critical resiliency engineering has been ignored while chasing feature releases. Brushing off a worldwide blackout as an unfortunate mistake while pivoting straight into sales mode is unacceptable for an infrastructure provider. Until leadership provides a comprehensive, transparent architectural accounting of why isolation failed at a planetary scale, every CIO and enterprise architect should treat their single-vendor exposure as an active operational liability. #CloudComputing #EnterpriseArchitecture #CloudReliability #Microsoft365 #CIO #TechStrategy #DisasterRecovery

story-74f42eae03c0031f47c13ceb.content: New Anthropic research: progress on provable inference for large language models. Here, we introduce FlashProve. Building on established cryptographic techniques, FlashProve allows developers to verify whether a given response came from a given AI model. It’s substantially more efficient than prior open-source methods for doing so. These proofs have a range of applications. They can, for instance, make it harder for attackers to hijack a chat, or enable safety evaluators to verify that the model they’re testing is the same one being served to customers. For our full write-up, see here: https://t.co/OIZWPb6QZa Further progress in provable inference will likely be an important part of improving trust in AI deployment. To that end, we're open-sourcing FlashProve’s code, here: https://t.co/7ky3Ir8V06 We’re grateful to our collaborators: Alessandro Chiesa, @GiacomoFenzi, @gwberg95, @miranda__christ, Rahul Dalal (https://t.co/pjWKLHWXyz) and Ben Mayer (@transmissions11).

story-7789a009e914690f483918b3.content: الهيئة السعودية للبيانات والذكاء الاصطناعي في تصريح لوكالة الأنباء السعودية عن الذكاء الاصطناعي العام (AGI) وخطط المملكة بشأنه: الوصول إلى الذكاء الاصطناعي العام لا يزال مسألة غير محسومة علميًا، في ظل اختلاف تعريفه وتباين تقديرات الخبراء بشأن إمكانية تحققه وتوقيت الوصول إليه. التطورات المتسارعة، وتحديدًا في الذكاء الاصطناعي التوليدي، دفعت إلى ظهور توقعات زمنية مختلفة، لكنها لا تمثل دليلًا قاطعًا على قرب الوصول إلى ذكاء يماثل القدرات البشرية العامة. التفاوت بين التقديرات يعكس ارتفاع مستوى عدم اليقين، وتأثر مسار التطور بعوامل عديدة تشمل التقدم التقني، والقدرات الحاسوبية، وحجم الاستثمارات، والبيئة التنظيمية؛ لذلك تتعامل المملكة مع الذكاء الاصطناعي العام بوصفه أحد السيناريوهات المستقبلية المحتملة التي تستوجب الاستعداد المبكر، دون ربط الجاهزية الوطنية بموعد محدد لظهوره.

story-794a30718878d2ff9e9d27c7.content: 13.000 bersagli colpiti in 38 giorni. Il software che ha aiutato a colpirli da venerdì, per decreto, si chiama «Super Intelligenza». Il 13 novembre il Pentagono ha cambiato nome al suo ufficio per l'intelligenza artificiale. La tecnologia è la stessa del giorno prima. È cambiata solo la parola. Perché? COSA È SUCCESSO Il Dipartimento della Guerra USA ha ribattezzato il Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO): ora è il Super Intelligence Office (SIO). Nuovo logo, nuovo sito https://t.co/BBflpGKh0y, nuovi social. Missione e programmi, dice il comunicato, restano identici. Il capo dell'ufficio, Cameron Stanley, ex Amazon Web Services ed ex capo di Project Maven, oggi Chief Super Intelligence Officer: «Abbiamo superato i prototipi sperimentali. La nostra missione è sfruttare tutta la potenza di una Super Intelligenza sovrana per garantire una superiorità militare decisiva in ogni dominio». Obiettivo dichiarato: un esercito «SI-First». UNA PAROLA NUOVA PER LA STESSA TECNOLOGIA Il cambio applica l'ordine esecutivo 14434, firmato da Trump il 29 settembre e pubblicato nel Federal Register il 2 ottobre: le agenzie federali devono scrivere «Super Intelligence» al posto di «Artificial Intelligence». I vecchi termini il governo «non li riconoscerà» più. Il dettaglio decisivo è all'articolo 3: «Super Intelligence» indica esattamente le tecnologie già coperte dalla definizione legale di intelligenza artificiale. Entro 60 giorni, cioè intorno al 28 novembre, il consigliere scientifico del presidente deve proporre al Congresso una definizione federale. Oggi non esiste. Breaking Defense lo ricorda: per gli esperti la superintelligenza è un'IA ipotetica che supera l'intelligenza umana. Non esiste ancora. COSA C'È DAVVERO DENTRO Sul sito https://t.co/BBflpGKh0y i programmi: • Maven Smart System, la piattaforma Palantir che fonde i dati dei sensori e rileva obiettivi in tempo reale • SI Tools: GPT di OpenAI, Gemini di Google e «GrokShield» in ambienti classificati • 7 progetti apripista: Swarm Forge, Agent Network (assistenti per gestione della battaglia e decisioni operative), Open Arsenal (nuove capacità militari «in ore invece che in anni») ed Ender's Foundry, l'IA nelle simulazioni militari Ender's Foundry richiama «Il gioco di Ender»: un ragazzo crede di giocare a una simulazione e comanda una guerra vera. MAVEN, I NUMERI Nasce nel 2017. Google si ritira nel 2018, subentra Palantir. Contratto alzato a quasi 1,3 miliardi di dollari fino al 2029. Utenti: circa 50.000 a gennaio 2026, oltre 100.000 a settembre. Secondo Stanley, durante l'operazione Epic Fury contro l'Iran Maven ha aiutato a colpire 13.000 bersagli in 38 giorni. Per il CSIS, oltre 1.000 nelle prime 24 ore: 10 volte quanto era possibile prima. L'operatore seleziona un bersaglio indicato dall'IA, un algoritmo propone e mette in classifica le armi da usare. CONFERMATO Il cambio di nome e l'ordine esecutivo 14434, pubblicato nel Federal Register. NON CONFERMATO I 13.000 bersagli sono un dato del capo dell'ufficio, senza verifica indipendente. Quanti siano stati controllati da una persona, e con quali tempi, non è pubblico. E L'ITALIA? Maven è usato anche dalla NATO, che dal 2025 ha una versione per il Comando Operazioni Alleato. E l'AI Act europeo, all'articolo 2, esclude i sistemi usati solo per scopi militari. Se per decreto la superintelligenza è già il software di oggi, come riconosceremo quella vera quando arriverà? E chi ha controllato quei 13.000 bersagli? Fonti e analisi completa: https://t.co/fsYPiv9TUK #Pentagono #IntelligenzaArtificiale

Imagine a world where algorithmic profiling turns military target selection into an automated "factory of targets," tracking individuals to their family homes before approving airstrikes. This is no future dystopia. The decisions that determine who lives and who dies in war are increasingly being made by machines. From November 16–20, governments meet in Geneva at the UN to consider opening negotiations on a treaty to regulate autonomous weapons. Regulation has failed to keep pace with reality. When the speed of AI-enabled operations leaves no time to verify targets, human control becomes a rubber stamp, triggering unlawful attacks and eroding accountability. States need to seize this moment to support urgent, time-bound negotiations for a global, legally binding instrument on autonomous weapons. Decisions over life and death should remain anchored in human judgement, responsibility and accountability, never delegated to machines. story-81f13f9c016e5c89ba6e5655.content: 🔴 كشفت شبكة «سي إن إن»، في تحقيق خاص يستند إلى أربعة مصادر مطلعة، أن الأعطال التقنية الواسعة التي أصابت وكالة الأمن القومي الأمريكية (NSA) طالت مركزاً استخبارياً حساساً في ولاية جورجيا، يتولى دعم عمليات استخبارات الإشارات والأمن السيبراني المرتبطة بالشرق الأوسط، بما في ذلك المنطقة التي تخوض فيها الولايات المتحدة الحرب مع إيران. وأدت الأعطال إلى تعطيل شبكة الاتصالات الداخلية السرية للوكالة، ومنعت العاملين في المركز من التواصل عبرها مع زملائهم المنتشرين في المنطقة، ما اضطرهم إلى استخدام قنوات بديلة لنقل المعلومات الاستخبارية. 🔷 واستمر تعطل العمل في بعض مرافق الوكالة لليوم الثاني، واضطرت الإدارة إلى مطالبة الموظفين غير الأساسيين في المقر الرئيسي بولاية ماريلاند بعدم الحضور يوم الأربعاء 18 نوفمبر. وأقر مسؤول رفيع في الإدارة الأمريكية بأن جهود استعادة الأنظمة تسير بوتيرة أبطأ من المتوقع. كما لاحظ مسؤولون في أجهزة استخبارية أمريكية أخرى انقطاع التواصل مع نظرائهم في وكالة الأمن القومي طوال يوم الثلاثاء. 🔷 تكمن أهمية مركز وكالة الأمن القومي في جورجيا، الموجود في قاعدة فورت غوردون، في إشرافه على عمليات سيبرانية واستخبارية موجهة نحو الشرق الأوسط. وأكد مسؤولون حاليون وسابقون أن العاملين فيه فقدوا القدرة على استخدام شبكة «إن إس إيه نت» (NSANet)، وهي منظومة الاتصالات الداخلية المصنفة سرياً التي تعتمد عليها الوكالة في تبادل التقارير والمعلومات بين مراكزها والعاملين المنتشرين خارج الولايات المتحدة. 🔷 أكدت مصادر أن انقطاع الشبكة أثّر في تدفق الاتصالات الاستخبارية المرتبطة بمنطقة عمليات عسكرية أمريكية نشطة، لكنه لم يؤدِّ إلى توقف عمليات جمع المعلومات الحساسة. فقد واصلت الأنظمة الاستخبارية الأكثر أهمية عملها، واستُخدمت قنوات احتياطية ووسائل بديلة لتبادل المعلومات. وأوضح مسؤول سابق أن ضابطاً أمريكياً في إحدى عواصم الشرق الأوسط قد يعجز مؤقتاً عن الوصول إلى تقرير سري عبر الشبكة المعتادة، لكنه يستطيع الحصول عليه من قناة أخرى. 🔷 كشف التحقيق أن البنية التقنية القديمة لوكالة الأمن القومي ساعدت، بصورة غير متوقعة، في احتواء نطاق العطل. فالعديد من شبكات الوكالة معزولة عن بعضها لأسباب أمنية واستخبارية، ولم تتأثر بالاضطرابات التي أصابت منظومة الاتصالات الرئيسية. وذكر مسؤول سابق أن شبكة «إن إس إيه نت» تطورت خلال عقود دون تصميم متكامل منذ البداية، وأصبحت منظومة ضخمة ومعقدة يصعب استبدالها بسبب الكلفة والجهد المطلوبين. 🔷 قدمت مصادر أمريكية تفسيراً تقنياً جديداً للأزمة، يرجح ارتباطها بمحاولات معالجة ثغرات أمنية في لغة البرمجة «بي إتش بي» (PHP)، وليس بهجوم سيبراني. وكانت جهات بحثية خاصة قد كشفت خلال أكتوبر ثغرات في هذه التقنية بمساعدة أدوات الذكاء الاصطناعي، ودعت وكالة الأمن القومي نفسها المؤسسات إلى تثبيت تحديثات أمنية لمعالجتها. وتشير المعلومات إلى أن عمليات تحديث الأنظمة ربما تسببت في اضطرابات تشغيلية داخل شبكة الوكالة. 🔷 أكد مسؤولون أمريكيون مطلعون أن التحقيقات لم تجد مؤشرات على تنفيذ هجوم إلكتروني ضد وكالة الأمن القومي. وأبلغ مدير الاستخبارات الوطنية جاي كلايتون أعضاء لجنة الأمن الداخلي في مجلس النواب بأنه يمتلك درجة ثقة مرتفعة جداً بأن الأعطال التي أصابت الأنظمة الحكومية والخاصة خلال الأسبوع لم تكن نتيجة عملية سيبرانية منسقة. وأوضح أن الحوادث نشأت عن أسباب مختلفة، وأن الفحص لم يكشف الأنماط التقنية المعروفة لعمليات الاختراق. 🔷 كشف التحقيق عن تحدٍّ جديد تواجهه المؤسسات الاستخبارية بسبب استخدام الذكاء الاصطناعي في اكتشاف الثغرات البرمجية بوتيرة غير مسبوقة. فقد حذر السيناتور مارك وارنر، نائب رئيس لجنة الاستخبارات في مجلس الشيوخ، من أن قدرة أدوات الذكاء الاصطناعي على اكتشاف ثغرات في أعداد هائلة من الأنظمة تفرض على المؤسسات تنفيذ تحديثات أمنية متزامنة وسريعة، ما يضع ضغطاً كبيراً على بنى تقنية لم تُصمم للتعامل مع هذه الوتيرة.

story-8214e5aed8977d08634d50ce.content: تكليف المهندس رائد القرني (مديرًا عامًا لاستعادة البيانات بعد الكوارث في السجل العقاري "RER") بالإضافة إلى مهام عمله مديرًا عامًا لمركز الخدمة. ◉ يتمتع المهندس رائد القرني @AbuJojo بخبرة واسعة تمتد لأكثر من 17 عامًا في مجالات تقنية المعلومات، وإدارة عمليات الخدمات التقنية، واستعادة البيانات بعد الكوارث، والتحول الرقمي، وإدارة المشاريع، وأمن المعلومات، وهندسة الشبكات، وإدارة مراكز البيانات، والقيادة، شغل خلالها عدد من المناصب القيادية، منها: •مدير إدارة الخدمات التقنية في السجل العقاري (RER). •مدير تقنية المعلومات في الكلية التقنية الدولية للطيران بالرياض. •مدير تقنية المعلومات بالإنابة في الكلية التقنية الدولية للطيران بالرياض. •مشرف تقنية معلومات في الكلية التقنية الدولية للطيران بالرياض. كما عمل أخصائي أول تقنية معلومات في شركة الطائرات المروحية وأخصائي تقنية معلومات في شركة السلام للصناعات الجوية”SAMI” شغل عدد من المناصب في الشركات التابعة لصندوق الاستثمارات العامة. ◉ بالإضافة إلى مناصبه القيادية، فقد شغل المهندس رائد القرني عضوية عدد من اللجان والمنظمات، من أبرزها: •عضو في FinTech 525 التابعة لجمعية التقنية المالية. •عضو في جمعية الذكاء الاصطناعي. •عضو في جمعية الحوسبة السحابية. •عضو مهندس في الهيئة السعودية للمهندسين. ◉ يحمل المهندس رائد القرني درجة الماجستير التنفيذي في التقنية المالية والابتكار من جامعة الملك سعود، ودرجة البكالوريوس في هندسة الحاسب والشبكات من كلية الاتصالات والمعلومات، ودبلوم في علوم الحاسب والشبكات من جامعة الإمام محمد بن سعود الإسلامية، ودبلوم في برنامج القادة الناشئين من كلية IE للأعمال، كما حصل على عدد من الشهادات المهنية المتخصصة، من أبرزها: •برنامج Leading with Finance من كلية هارفارد للأعمال. •شهادة المهارات الإدارية الأساسية من المعهد الدولي للإدارة (IBMI). •برنامج Leading Digital Transformation من كلية لندن للأعمال. •شهادة Finance for Non-Financials من أكاديمية الحوكمة. •شهادة المسؤول الدولي المعتمد في الحوكمة المؤسسية (ICCGO) من AGRC. •شهادة مدقق داخلي معتمد ISO 9001:2015. •شهادة مدقق نظم معلومات معتمد Certified Associate information systems auditor CISA. •شهادة ISO 20000 Lead Implementer و Lead Auditor. •شهادة ITIL®️ 4 Foundation CPD. •شهادة محترف إدارة مراكز البيانات المعتمد (CDCMP). •شهادة Cyber Security Foundation Professional Certificate (CSFPC). •شهادة CCNA من سيسكو. •شهادة تحديد التهديدات الأمنية والثغرات من شركة السلام للصناعات الجوية.

story-83938c4b3e52c062c4c1c99f.content: #عاجل | عُقد اليوم (الاثنين) منتدى للتعمّق والتعلّم في موضوع الذكاء الاصطناعي، برئاسة رئيس الأركان، الجنرال إيال زامير، وبمشاركة أعضاء هيئة الأركان العامة وقادة الألوية، في مقرّ الاتصالات والحوسبة الجديد في مدينة بئر السبع. 🔹خلال المنتدى، عُرضت على القادة سبل دمج قدرات الذكاء الاصطناعي (AI) في منظومات الدفاع والهجوم التابعة لجيش الدفاع، واستخدام هذه التقنيات لمعالجة المعلومات وتحليلها، وتحسين إجراءات العمل، وزيادة الكفاءة التنظيمية والعملياتية. من أقوال رئيس الأركان، الجنرال إيال زامير: 🔹“الذكاء الاصطناعي ثورة تُغيّر ملامح القرن الحادي والعشرين. 🔹تتقدّم التكنولوجيا بوتيرة سريعة، وتُعيد تشكيل أساليب التفكير والعمل في جميع المجالات. كما أن طبيعة ساحة المعركة تتغيّر بوتيرة سريعة. 🔹تشهد ساحة المعركة في السنوات الأخيرة أحد أسرع التغيّرات وأعمقها وأكثرها دراماتيكية في التاريخ العسكري. 🔹من أجل مواجهة تحديات الحرب وتحقيق الحسم، تقع على عاتق جيش الدفاع مسؤولية وواجب بأن يكون رائدًا عالميًا في الابتكار والتغيير، بما في ذلك استيعاب القدرات المتقدمة في مجال الذكاء الاصطناعي والروبوتات وإدماجها. 🔹لا يقتصر الابتكار على التكنولوجيا فحسب؛ فمن أجل اعتماد أنماط عمل مبتكرة، لا بدّ من قيادة شجاعة ورائدة تشقّ آفاقًا جديدة، ومن تبنّي ثقافة الانفتاح القادرة على تغيير أنماط التفكير والتغيّر. 🔹القادة الذين لن يعرفوا كيف يوظّفون التكنولوجيا لصالحهم لن ينجحوا في تنفيذ مهامهم في ساحة المعركة الحديثة. 🔹يفرض علينا الواقع الأمني الاستعداد لمواجهة التحديات في عدة ساحات في الوقت نفسه. ويشكّل الذكاء الاصطناعي عنصرًا أساسيًا في استعدادنا للعمل في ساحات متعددة، إذ يعزّز قدرات الاستخبارات واتخاذ القرارات والعمل. 🔹إن القرارات المتعلقة بإنشاء ذراع جديدة للذكاء الاصطناعي والوسائل غير المأهولة، وإنشاء لواء الذكاء الاصطناعي ولواء الطيف في هيئة الاتصالات والحوسبة والدفاع السيبراني، تعزّز حرية عمل جيش الدفاع في جميع الساحات، وتتيح لنا قدرات جديدة ورائدة. 🔹في إطار مفهوم عملياتي مبتكر، سيعزز جيش الدفاع ويطوّر مفهوم القتال المشترك بين الإنسان والآلة، حيث ستقاتل وحدات مأهولة بالتكامل مع وسائل غير مأهولة لتحقيق التفوق والأفضلية العملياتية في ساحة المعركة. 🔹في إطار خطة بناء القوة متعددة السنوات “حوشن”، يعمل جيش الدفاع على تعزيز إدماج قدرات الذكاء الاصطناعي (AI) في مختلف مجالات النشاط العسكري. 🔹نعقد هذا اليوم في مقرّ الاتصالات والحوسبة الذي أُنشئ في مدينة بئر السبع. قال بن غوريون إن شعب إسرائيل سيُختبر في النقب، وإن هذا الجهد سيحدّد مصير دولة إسرائيل. ونحن اليوم نحقّق هذه الرؤية. 🔹فهيئة الاتصالات والحوسبة، وهيئة الاستخبارات العسكرية، وهيئة التكنولوجيا واللوجستيات، وسلاح الجو موجودة هنا في إطار تحقيق هذه الرؤية. 🔹إن مستقبل جيش الدفاع ومستقبل النقب مرتبطان أحدهما بالآخر”.

story-83e77bf1e2c8339238310cdd.content: Grok on the topic of targeted ads location exploit recently: Device identifiers, precise location data, and other signals that leak through the advertising ecosystem. This is not traditional “ads” in the sense of the image or text you see. It is the real-time bidding (RTB) process and the data brokers behind it. When an app or website loads an ad slot, it broadcasts information about the device and user to bidders in milliseconds. That data is routinely collected, packaged, and sold. Intelligence services and private surveillance firms (including many Israeli ones) buy access to it or inject themselves into the system. What specifically is harvested? - Mobile Advertising IDs (AAID on Android, IDFA on iOS) — persistent device identifiers. - Precise GPS / location coordinates from apps that share them with ad networks or data brokers (weather, games, navigation, prayer apps, etc.). - IP addresses, browser cookies, and device fingerprints. - Behavioral signals that allow cross-site tracking and pattern-of-life mapping. The same pipeline that lets an advertiser target “people who looked at running shoes near this mall” lets a buyer track a phone’s movements over time, link it to other identifiers, or aim further collection at it. US Central Command confirmed in 2026 that adversaries have used commercially available location data of this type to target or surveil US personnel in active war zones. Recent documented cases involving Israeli-linked actors: In October 2026, Citizen Lab and the ad-security firm Confiant published findings on **Discover-Tech**, an Israeli company that presented itself as an ad buyer. It used ordinary-looking ads (phones, earbuds, etc.) across hundreds of thousands of sites and apps. - Simply loading one of their ads could transmit identifiers and allow profiling. - For selected targets, the system delivered zero-click Candiru (now Integrity Labs) spyware — no tap required. Citizen Lab linked this to at least 45 Windows devices at Al Jazeera. - The firm’s ads were especially dense in the Palestinian territories, giving broad visibility into digital activity there. Researchers also noted heavy interest in Starlink users in conflict zones (Syria, Libya, Yemen, etc.), where legitimate Western advertising demand is low. - Impressions appeared on sensitive networks including those associated with the Pentagon, NATO, the UN, the ICC, and various government and tech entities. This fits a broader pattern. Multiple Israeli firms (often founded by Unit 8200 veterans) sell “advertising intelligence” (ADINT) tools that turn the commercial ad ecosystem into a surveillance feed. Other countries’ intelligence services do the same thing with the same data brokers. Why it works in war areas In conflict zones the commercial data is often easier to obtain and more valuable than traditional signals intelligence for certain tasks: mapping movements of phones, identifying clusters, tracking specific devices across SIMs or apps, or feeding AI targeting systems. Apps keep collecting and selling location even when users think they have restricted permissions, and the ad auction system is designed to share it widely. This is the same underlying mechanism that makes it hard to fully lock down location data on an Android while running gig apps — those apps (and the ad SDKs many of them include) are feeding the same commercial pipeline that intelligence and surveillance customers buy from. Restricting non-essential app permissions and turning off location history reduces some of the volume, but it does not eliminate the signals the ad ecosystem already collects and sells.

story-84552a9d3b7956232828da94.content: 🇷🇺 Rusia lanza al espacio satélites de compañías privadas por primera vez El 14 de noviembre, desde el cosmódromo Vostochni, se lanzó el cohete Soyuz-2.1b, que puso en órbita dos satélites de observación: KOEN de la empresa MT-LAB y Kinosputnik del grupo de empresas Sputniks. KOEN está diseñado para obtener imágenes de la superficie terrestre con una resolución de hasta 0,5 metros por píxel, lo cual se asemeja a las posibilidades de la empresa china MizarVision. El aparato está diseñado para operar a una altitud de aproximadamente 500 km y es capaz de fotografiar una franja de superficie de hasta 12 km de ancho. Kinosputnik está equipado con una cámara multiespectral con una resolución de 0,8 metros por píxel. La masa del aparato es de aproximadamente 200 kg. La empresa Sputniks ya ha informado de la recepción de telemetría del Kinosputnik. Según el desarrollador, sus sistemas a bordo están funcionando correctamente. La particularidad de este lanzamiento es que el Estado ha financiado parcialmente, por primera vez, la puesta en órbita de satélites privados, en el marco del proyecto nacional Cosmos. 🔺 ¿Para qué sirven los nuevos satélites? (A nivel civil) ▪️ Controlar la construcción y el estado de la infraestructura. ▪️ Monitorear el uso de la tierra y las tierras agrícolas. ▪️ Realizar un seguimiento de las áreas naturales. ▪️ Identificar construcciones ilegales, vertederos y canteras. ▪️ Evaluar las consecuencias de incendios, inundaciones y otras situaciones de emergencia. Esto crea un mecanismo en el que las empresas comerciales desarrollan y operan sus propios aparatos, mientras que el Estado compensa parte de los gastos de su lanzamiento y obtiene la posibilidad de utilizar los resultados de la observación espacial.

story-84d386c29200aaee0261475d.content: Are We Seeing More Outages, Or Just Looking Harder? One of the more interesting things about the recent wave of outage stories is not just the outages themselves. It’s the psychology around them. There’s a well-known cognitive bias called the frequency illusion, or the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon. You buy a certain car, and suddenly that car seems to be everywhere. The car did not necessarily become more common overnight. You just started noticing it. I think some of that is happening right now with cloud and SaaS outages. The recent Microsoft outage was different. It was large, highly visible, and disruptive enough that it deserved the attention it received. Reports described Microsoft 365 services such as Outlook and Teams being affected across many countries, with restoration taking far longer than anyone should consider acceptable for systems that many businesses now treat as critical infrastructure: https://t.co/TPaGu2fZun [1] But once an event like that hits the front page, everyone starts watching the sky. After Jaws came out in the 1970s, shark sightings and shark fears became part of the public consciousness in a much bigger way. The sharks were not new. The attention was. That’s where I think we need to be careful with the current outage narrative. Outages happen all the time. Failed deployments, capacity issues, DNS problems, expired certificates, degraded regions, bot traffic, security probing, and authentication issues are part of the operating reality of modern distributed systems. Most do not become national news because, frankly, they are not unusual. So are we seeing an actual uptick? Maybe. Cloud systems are more complex. Dependencies are more concentrated. AI workloads are putting new stress on infrastructure. Companies have cut costs, consolidated platforms, and built business processes around a small number of providers. That does increase systemic risk. But are we also paying more attention because Microsoft kicked off a news cycle? Absolutely. Both things can be true. My concern is not that every outage in the press signals a collapse of cloud reliability. It does not. My concern is that many enterprises still treat resilience as something their provider owns entirely. That is the real issue. The right takeaway is not panic. It’s architecture. Assume your cloud provider will fail. Assume your SaaS platform will be unavailable. Assume identity, email, collaboration, and security tools can go down at the same time. Then ask the uncomfortable question: can the business still operate? If the answer is no, the problem is not just the outage. The problem is the design.

story-854d78b767806388416da41a.content: ❗️THE BANKING OUTAGES ARE NOT GLITCHES. THE LEGACY CLEARING SYSTEM IS FRACTURING A payment infrastructure engineer shared the internal incident tickets with me less than an hour ago. Five Tier-1 banks. Two continents. Core settlement nodes going dark without a single public root-cause report. Here is what the incident logs actually show: * It is not a simple cyber attack. It is a structural failure. Firewalls are not the only thing breaking-interbank trust is breaking * It is not temporary downtime. It is a liquidity freeze. Transfers are not queued for convenience. They are queued because the backing is missing * It is not an isolated weekend patch. It is a cascading bottleneck. When one clearing house stalls, three others lose their collateral bridge * It is not going back to normal. It is the end of unbacked digital entries. The era of endless credit creation just hit a hard wall ⚠️WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU: 1. DO NOT TRUST "ROUTINE MAINTENANCE" NOTICES * When a major bank locks out transfers for 12 hours, it is not upgrading its app * It is buying time while the back-end ledger fails to reconcile 2. STOP LEAVING EVERYTHING IN LEGACY PAPER * Numbers on a commercial banking screen are only promises until you try to move them at scale * Those who diversified into real, asset-backed channels are not panicking when the portals freeze 3. WATCH THE INTERBANK SPREADS * When banks stop lending to each other overnight, the system is already in cardiac arrest * The freeze happens behind closed doors long before ATMs go offline 4. EXPECT MORE "CYBER INCIDENTS" THIS WEEK * Every system collapse needs a cover story. "External attacks" are the easiest excuse for an empty vault * Look past the headline. Look at which institutions can actually settle ✨For decades, the world was told the banking network was unbreakable. It was unbreakable. Until the liquidity dried up. And it is drying up right now. 📱FORWARD THIS POST TO SOMEONE WHO STILL THINKS THEIR BANK APP IS INVINCIBLE. They need to understand what is happening. They need to stop ignoring the warning signs. They need to see the shift before the gates close. The old rails are buckling under their own weight. The only question is whether you positioned yourself before the next outage hits. __________________________ [FOLLOW THE SIGNAL] Christian B. Wallace Tier 4B

story-8784f7f86eed9e6822d0ff6e.content: Je ne suis pas toujours d'accord avec LeCun sur les usages et les capacités des LLM. Mais lui faire porter le retard de Meta sur les LLM, je ne suis pas d'accord non plus. Chez Meta, il avait de l'influence, mais ce n'est pas lui qui pilotait les LLM : Llama 2 à 4 ont été faits par GenAI, une équipe séparée de FAIR, le labo qu'il dirigeait. Ses travaux à lui portent sur JEPA et les world models, et il répète depuis des années que les LLM ne suffiront pas pour atteindre une IA de niveau humain. C'est son point de vue, on peut être d'accord ou pas, mais c'est le sien depuis le début. FAIR, le labo qu'il a fondé, a quand même donné PyTorch, sur lequel tourne une bonne partie de l'IA actuelle. Et c'est de FAIR que viennent Guillaume Lample et Timothée Lacroix, deux des cofondateurs de Mistral. Pour l'IA française, ce n'est pas rien. La réponse de Zuckerberg au raté de Llama 4, c'est Meta Superintelligence Labs, confié à Alexandr Wang, le fondateur de Scale AI, et FAIR y a ensuite été rattaché. Avec le départ de LeCun quelques mois plus tard, on peut y voir une passation. Mais Wang n'est pas un remplaçant de LeCun : c'est un autre métier, dans une maison entièrement restructurée. Sur le fait qu'AMI Labs n'ait encore rien sorti : le labo a été lancé le 10 mars 2026, et sa direction annonçait dès le départ environ un an avant les premiers usages produit. Huit mois sans produit, c'est simplement le calendrier prévu. Pour moi, les LLM, aussi bluffants soient-ils, ne sont qu'une étape. Pour aller vers l'AGI et déployer massivement l'IA dans des processus messy et exigeants, il faudra sans doute d'autres briques, et les world models de LeCun en sont une piste sérieuse. Il peut se tromper, mais c'est ce qu'on demande à un chercheur comme lui : prendre des paris. On ne gagne pas à tous les coups, mais il donne beaucoup d'espoir, par ce qu'il apportera probablement à l'état de l'art et par ce qu'il insuffle. On a besoin de gens comme lui dans l'IA. Meta s'en sortait très bien avec lui et s'en sort encore sans lui. Lui a un prix Turing, vient de lever 1 Md$, la plus grosse levée seed d'Europe, avec des acteurs comme Samsung, et s'est donné pour mission de prouver ce qu'il avance. Depuis la France. donc oui, il peut l'ouvrir s'il veut, et on peut être d'accord ou pas.

story-878c3590c517ec6606c4f712.content: 🚨 BREAKING: Your Smart TV May Be SPYING ON YOU Even After You Turn Tracking OFF. Researchers at Northeastern University just uncovered disturbing privacy issues affecting some of the world’s biggest TV brands, including Samsung, Vizio, and Roku. They conducted 5,943 experiments across 12 smart TVs and discovered that some devices continued communicating with tracking servers even after users explicitly opted out. Here’s what they found: → Samsung: Traffic consistent with tracking continued even after users disabled the feature, including when watching content through HDMI. → Vizio: 100% of tested opt-out runs continued sending traffic to its identified tracking endpoint, with no observable reduction. → Roku: Its privacy opt-out doesn’t cover its own streaming service. → 57 MILLION+ RECORDS EXPOSED: Researchers discovered an unauthenticated server containing over 57 million content recognition results linked to more than 1 million unique TVs. → UNENCRYPTED VIEWING DATA: VIDAA TVs transmitted device identifiers, audio fingerprints, app names, and viewing information without encryption. → YOUR HDMI INPUT ISN’T PRIVATE: Some TVs can identify content playing through connected devices, not just built-in streaming apps. The technology behind this is called Automatic Content Recognition (ACR). It captures audio or video fingerprints from what’s playing on your television, sends them to remote servers, and identifies the content for purposes including advertising and audience tracking. Even more concerning, researchers found that Vizio’s WatchFree+ service exposed program titles through network requests, potentially allowing network observers to reconstruct viewing histories. Important distinction: Much of the tracking traffic was encrypted, so researchers could not confirm what Samsung or Vizio actually collected after opt-out. The exposed VIDAA server has since been secured with authentication, although its ACR transmissions reportedly remain unencrypted. Your television isn’t necessarily just displaying what you’re watching. It may also be reporting it. And apparently, pressing “Don’t Track Me” isn’t always enough. story-880414f13f888fb20f610fad.content: 🚨 Microsoft has declared CODE RED after a hidden bug brought Microsoft 365 to its knees worldwide. Understand What Happened: 👇 > A Windows defect introduced in July went undetected due to differences between test and production hardware. > On November 12, 14% of gateway capacity was offline, Teams traffic was shifted to shared Exchange gateways, and peak traffic hit. > CPU and memory got exhausted, triggering automatic failovers that spread the outage across regions in under 2 hours. > Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, Exchange Online and Copilot were disrupted across 70+ countries. > The outage lasted nearly 24 hours, with recovery continuing until November 14. 🔴 Why is Microsoft declaring CODE RED? > Internal memos revealed that the affected component had consumed roughly 10 years' worth of acceptable failures. Microsoft's new priorities: - Global fixes in under 1 hour. - Better traffic management and failure isolation. - AI-powered incident diagnosis. - Improved crisis communication. DevOps Lesson To Learn: - One hidden bug + traffic overload + poor failure isolation = global outage. - Test on production-like hardware. - Control blast radius. - Test automatic failovers. - Maintain independent backup systems. Even Microsoft isn't immune to downtime. Does your organization have a backup plan when its primary cloud provider goes down?

story-8a558f2d1cf3081cd3bdb1f7.content: We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life. Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown. With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery. Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells. For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science. In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them. Read more: https://t.co/KowVVCSPp8

story-8a9b1a56f8d739e625acba24.content: Eight years after employee protests pushed Google to let its Project Maven contract expire, the company is back in talks with the Pentagon. This time, it's about data security for the $185B Golden Dome missile defense program. The interesting part is how different the role looks this time. Back in 2018, Project Maven was easy to understand. Google was helping the Pentagon analyze drone footage using AI. Employees knew exactly what they were protesting, and the company eventually let the contract expire. Golden Dome is a different story. There's no single contractor building the entire system. It's a collection of companies, each responsible for a different part of the project. Google's potential role is much less visible. The discussions reportedly focus on data storage, networking and cybersecurity, essentially keeping military command-and-control systems connected if landlines or cellular networks are taken out. This isn't about building weapons. It's about providing the infrastructure behind them. And that's a much harder thing to draw a line around. Google already sells cloud storage and networking services to businesses around the world. Now those same capabilities could become part of a military defense system. It's also worth looking at what happened in April. Google agreed to make its AI models available on classified Pentagon networks. There was some employee backlash, but nothing close to the reaction to Project Maven. Google's networking spinoff, Aalyria, is also involved in the Golden Dome consortium. There are still plenty of caveats. These are early discussions, not a signed contract. The Pentagon says no final decisions have been made, and both Google and Aalyria declined to comment. But I think the bigger question is what happens after a company gets this kind of foothold. Once your infrastructure becomes part of a system's core operations, replacing you isn't exactly easy. And when the next contract comes along, expanding your role becomes a much smaller step. Google may be entering through data storage and networking rather than weapons development. But infrastructure can be just as important as the systems it supports. That's what makes this shift worth watching. #GoldenDome #Google #DefenseTech

story-8a9bf5ff72bd12e83177269b.content: Cheap energy is becoming a competitive advantage in the global race to attract data centers. Sara Eisen’s point, echoed by Jim Cramer, is that Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Canada are promoting access to lower-cost energy alongside faster and easier permitting. For AI infrastructure, electricity is not a secondary operating expense. It is a core input that can determine where a project is economically viable. The competition is therefore about more than tax incentives: power prices, grid capacity, construction timelines and regulatory certainty all matter. story-8f28545946b7e86ce0ca6b40.content: He said the fourth thing he changed was the HDMI port setting, because her streaming box was plugged into a port that wasn’t set to its full bandwidth. He said this one sounds technical, but it’s often the reason 4K HDR doesn’t look right, or a console doesn’t run at its full refresh rate. “Many TVs ship with their HDMI ports set to a standard mode. To use the full bandwidth, you have to set the port to Enhanced. It’s called HDMI Deep Color on some TVs, Input Signal Plus on others, and HDMI Enhanced or HDMI Format on others. It unlocks 4K HDR, Dolby Vision, 120Hz, and full color from a game console, an Apple TV, or a streaming stick. If you don’t turn it on, the TV may fall back to a lower quality signal without telling you.” He said to set it: on a Hisense, it’s Settings → System → HDMI & CEC → HDMI Format → Enhanced. On an LG, it’s under General → Devices → HDMI Settings, per port. Check your manual for the name on your TV. Also, many TVs only have two or so ports with full bandwidth, so put your best device in the right one. “Use a certified Ultra High Speed HDMI cable. A cheap cable can cause random black screens once the port is running at full speed.” He said for gaming, turn on Game Mode, and enable Auto Low Latency Mode, or ALLM, on the console’s input. “That switches off the extra processing and brings most modern TVs to very low input lag. She doesn’t game, but her son does, and he said it made a difference right away.”

story-90346f88f6c03baf44ae1f47.content: Espionnage en orbite et pouvoir de l’information : https://t.co/fYMh40Ijgt "Traduction en français : Résumé Les satellites de reconnaissance permettent d’observer l’état des installations militaires d’un État cible sans pénétrer dans son espace aérien souverain. Les informations ainsi obtenues peuvent influencer des opérations militaires menées à plusieurs milliers de kilomètres de distance. Toutefois, l’observation d’un territoire, l’intervention dans des systèmes bénéficiant d’une protection juridique, le soutien apporté aux parties à un conflit et l’emploi de la force constituent des actes distincts, assortis de conséquences juridiques différentes. Il n’existe donc pas de règle unique de droit international susceptible de résoudre de manière uniforme l’ensemble de ces questions. Le présent article examine dans quelles circonstances les informations recueillies en orbite cessent d’être une simple source d’avantage stratégique pour devenir un acte juridiquement significatif. À travers une analyse dogmatique du droit de l’espace, de la Charte des Nations Unies, du droit de la responsabilité internationale des États et du droit international humanitaire, l’étude développe le cadre conceptuel de la « conversion juridique de l’information ». Ce cadre examine les situations dans lesquelles l’acquisition, la diffusion ou l’utilisation opérationnelle de données satellitaires se rattache à des obligations spécifiques de droit international. En s’appuyant sur des sources publiques relatives aux programmes de satellites de reconnaissance de la péninsule coréenne, au système satellitaire israélien Ofek 19 et aux images satellitaires fournies commercialement à l’Ukraine, l’article met en lumière à la fois l’importance militaire de l’observation depuis l’orbite et les limites inhérentes à tout raisonnement juridique fondé sur des informations ouvertes. L’article rejette l’assimilation immédiate d’une observation étrangère à une attaque armée, tout en récusant l’idée selon laquelle la liberté des activités dans l’espace extra-atmosphérique exonérerait automatiquement toute utilisation ultérieure de l’information de toute responsabilité juridique. Il propose une approche juridique fondée sur les circonstances factuelles concrètes, de nature à protéger les intérêts de sécurité des États souverains, à préserver les conditions juridiques du recours à la force en légitime défense et à prendre en compte les effets sur les populations civiles dépendantes de services spatiaux communs." "偵察衛星は、対象国の領空に侵入することなく軍事施設の状況を把握することができ、そこから得られた情報は、数千キロメートル離れた場所で実施される軍事作戦に影響を与える可能性がある。しかし、領域の観測、法的保護の対象となるシステムへの介入、交戦当事者への支援、および武力の行使は、それぞれ異なる法的帰結を伴う行為であるため、これらをめぐる問題を一律に解決する単一の国際法規則は存在しない。本論文は、軌道上で収集された情報が、単なる戦略的優位性の源泉を超えて、いかなる状況において法的に重要な行為となるのかを検討するものである。 本研究では、宇宙法、国際連合憲章、国家責任法および国際人道法に関する法教義学的分析を通じて、「情報の法的転換」という概念的枠組みを展開する。これは、衛星データの取得、流通または作戦上の利用が、特定可能な国際法上の義務と結び付く状況を検討するものである。朝鮮半島における偵察衛星計画、イスラエルのOfek 19衛星システム、およびウクライナに商業的に提供された衛星画像に関する公開資料を用い、軌道上からの観測が有する軍事的重要性と、公開情報に基づいて法的推論を行う際の限界の双方を明らかにする。 本論文は、外国による観測行為を直ちに武力攻撃と同一視する考え方を退ける一方、宇宙空間における活動の自由によって、その後の情報利用がすべて法的責任から免除されるという見解も否定する。そして、主権国家の安全保障上の利益を保護しつつ、自衛のための武力行使に関する法的要件を維持し、さらに共通の宇宙サービスに依存する民間人への影響にも配慮する、具体的事実関係に即した法的対応のあり方を提示する。" "1 Orbital Espionage and the Power of Information State Sovereignty, Military Intelligence and the Limits of Self-Defence under International Law Silvio Moreira Alves Júnior Brazilian Attorney - Independent Researcher silviojr.adv@outlook.com https://t.co/08Urt6Tvur 2026 Abstract Orbital reconnaissance has intensified legal questions surrounding the observation of strategic assets, the circulation of satellite-derived information and its use in military decision-making. This article examines the relationship between space-based intelligence, State sovereignty and the legal frameworks applicable to international conduct. The central research question concerns the circumstances in which the collection, transfer or operational employment of orbital information requires legal assessment under international law. The study adopts a qualitative, doctrinal and documentary approach based on the Outer Space Treaty, the Charter of the United Nations, the law of State responsibility and relevant rules of international humanitarian law. Publicly available material concerning Korean reconnaissance programmes, Israel’s Ofek 19 satellite and commercial satellite imagery provided in connection with the conflict in Ukraine is considered as documentary context. The Theory of Dynamic Adaptive Warfare is used to situate the strategic role of information while keeping the doctrinal legal analysis analytically distinct. The discussion addresses the jurisdictional framework for orbital observation, the participation of public and private actors, the scope and limits of the documentary record, and the legal standards relevant to possible State responses. 2 Keywords: Orbital Espionage. State Sovereignty. Military Intelligence. Law. War. Space. International Space Law. Self-defence. 1. Introduction: The State That Can Be Seen but Cannot Exclude the Observer Sovereignty traditionally gives a State authority over its territory and the airspace above it, yet orbital observation has made a portion of its most sensitive security environment visible to foreign governments without a conventional border crossing. A military base can remain inaccessible to outsiders on the ground while its construction, patterns of movement and apparent operational readiness become the subject of repeated satellite collection. The contradiction is not that sovereignty has disappeared or that outer space belongs to whoever possesses the strongest satellites. It is that the ability to obtain consequential knowledge has become partly separated from the territorial power to prevent physical entry, creating a legal dispute that begins with information but can end with coercion. Treating the subject only as espionage would miss the character of this separation; treating it only as space law would miss the consequences of turning an image into a military decision. The central research question is therefore narrower and more difficult than whether reconnaissance satellites are generally lawful: under what conditions can the acquisition or use of information collected from orbit constitute an internationally relevant wrong, and what remedies remain available to the State whose security is exposed? The proposed answer is that strategic sensitivity is not itself a source of international prohibition. Legal relevance emerges when a particular method of collection, intervention in another State's protected interests, attributable assistance to unlawful conduct or operation in an armed conflict satisfies the elements of an applicable rule. This distinction is consequential because a State may know with confidence that it is being watched while lacking evidence of a specific breach, and the temptation to close that 3 evidentiary gap with the language of self-defence risks converting insecurity into an asserted entitlement to force. The analysis is doctrinal and documentary rather than quantitative. It interprets the Outer Space Treaty alongside the Charter of the United Nations, the International Law Commission's rules on State responsibility and the law of armed conflict, then compares that framework with limited but verifiable public records of contemporary reconnaissance systems. The article draws on the Theory of Dynamic Adaptive Warfare (TDAW) to explain why information changes military choice, and on earlier work on orbital sovereignty to identify the jurisdictional setting, without reproducing a theory of orbital escalation or attempting to measure the probability of conflict (Alves Júnior, 2026a, 2026b). Its distinct contribution is a juridical account of informational advantage: knowledge may alter a State's vulnerability profoundly while the grounds for responsibility and the lawful range of responses remain questions to be established separately. 2. The Jurisdictional Paradox of Remote Observation Article 1 of the Chicago Convention establishes complete and exclusive sovereignty in the airspace above national territory, but the law applicable to outer space does not simply extend this territorial model upward indefinitely. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 protects freedom of exploration and use in Article I, excludes national appropriation through sovereign claims in Article II and requires conformity with international law, including the United Nations Charter, in Article III (International Civil Aviation Organization, 1944; United Nations, 1967). Neither instrument establishes an agreed numerical boundary between airspace and outer space, which means that analysis should not quietly assume a fixed internationally accepted altitude. For activities conducted in what States consistently treat as orbital space, however, it would be misleading to describe each passage over foreign territory as the equivalent of an unauthorised 4 reconnaissance aircraft entering sovereign airspace. The observer does not acquire territorial authority by orbiting, but the observed State does not acquire an automatic territorial veto over the orbit. This allocation of freedoms leaves a politically uncomfortable but legally important result. The target of observation may have legitimate national-security interests, and those interests may be put at risk by the accumulation of images that disclose patterns no single photograph would reveal. Yet injury to secrecy is not identical to a violation of sovereignty, because international law does not establish a comprehensive right to exclude all observation of territory from space. The principle of non-intervention requires attention to coercive interference in matters reserved to a State, not merely to the existence of foreign interest in those matters. Satellite reconnaissance may support later unlawful interference, but a legal conclusion about that later interference cannot be projected backwards onto the orbit as if the collection itself necessarily contained every element of the subsequent offence. The 1986 Principles Relating to Remote Sensing of the Earth from Outer Space require a careful qualification. Their definition of remote sensing is tied to improving natural-resource management, land use and environmental protection, so they cannot simply be transposed to classified military reconnaissance. Within that defined field, the principles address respect for sensed States, cooperation and access to primary and processed data on non-discriminatory and reasonable-cost terms (United Nations General Assembly, 1986, principles I and XII). They are General Assembly principles rather than a treaty conferring a general veto over satellite observation, and they do not establish an unconditional right to obtain classified military imagery. Their relevance to the present inquiry is therefore contextual rather than determinative: they demonstrate the international concern for the interests of observed States while leaving any 5 allegation concerning military intelligence to be examined under the law actually applicable to that conduct. The relevance of sovereignty is clearest when a dispute is framed as a demand to control the intelligence product rather than a demand to control the orbit. Information about a military installation may be sensitive, expensive to conceal and capable of informing coercive diplomacy, yet international law has not established an exclusive property right held by the territorial State over every representation of its territory produced from outside its jurisdiction. A claim founded only on the State's preference for secrecy therefore differs from a claim founded on unlawful entry, a binding confidentiality obligation or harmful interference with a protected system. That distinction need not disable diplomacy or domestic regulation. States may protect military sites against unauthorised access, regulate classified disclosures within their jurisdiction and employ counterintelligence, but they cannot infer from those domestic authorities an extraterritorial power to prohibit all observation from outer space. Defining the legal interest accurately makes both claims and restraint more credible, because it leaves room for a right to object to genuinely unlawful conduct without constructing a sovereignty rule that treaty practice does not support. That distinction also clarifies the role of Article IX of the Outer Space Treaty, which calls for due regard to corresponding interests and provides for consultations concerning activities that may cause potentially harmful interference. Due regard is not a general authorisation for a sensed State to forbid all strategically unwelcome information-gathering, but neither is freedom of use a licence to disregard harm, dangerous proximity operations or interference with other space systems. A satellite that observes passively and one that intentionally disrupts a spacecraft's communications may occupy the same orbital environment while presenting legally different questions. The 6 operative facts are the conduct, effects, applicable obligations and evidence of any interference, not the adjective 'military' attached to the mission. 3. Information as an Object of Power, Not an Automatic International Wrong Intelligence is valuable because it reshapes the choices available to institutions that can use it. Persistent observation can reduce uncertainty about deployment, reveal a departure from ordinary activity, corroborate information from human sources or expose deception. The reduction of uncertainty is not equivalent to certainty about intent: a photograph can document the presence of an object without establishing why it is present, whether the activity is lawful or what a commander intends to do next. This difference becomes even more important when remote-sensing products are combined with communications interception, public sources and algorithmic analysis. A sophisticated intelligence picture may be strategically persuasive yet incapable, by itself, of proving the legal elements of a prohibited act. The concept of informational power developed here is relational rather than proprietary. The State collecting data gains potential influence over its own decisions and sometimes over an ally's conduct, while the State observed loses a measure of practical secrecy without necessarily losing any jurisdiction recognised by international law. These consequences should not be confused. Intelligence about missile movements could serve strategic warning, verification, targeting or diplomatic de-escalation, and the legal assessment changes when the information is used in a course of conduct that international law regulates. An image does not carry a fixed legal character through every subsequent transaction. The same dataset can be lawfully collected, contractually transferred, misinterpreted, relied upon in an unlawful attack or used to prevent an attack on civilians; determining its significance requires examining identifiable actions and actors rather than assigning liability to 'information' as an abstraction. 7 A different risk arises when analysts and officials move from a claim of strategic harm to a claim of legal injury without identifying the obligation said to have been broken. The possibility that foreign intelligence will be used against national security is real, but the fact of that possibility cannot eliminate the difference between evidence of observation and evidence of prohibited coercion. Nor should this analysis imply that all intelligence methods are immune from challenge. Intrusion into sovereign airspace, harmful interference with satellites, violations of specific international commitments and military operations prohibited by the law of force may be unlawful even when motivated by intelligence collection. The article's point is not to protect espionage as a legal category; it is to avoid using that contested label in place of the legal elements that must actually be demonstrated. This account gives the TDAW an appropriately limited function. The theory explains war as an adaptive environment in which information and human judgement condition action across domains, but the legal argument in this article does not depend on proving a forecast of escalation or importing a full theory of conflict into every doctrinal issue (Alves Júnior, 2026b). The informational advantage generated in orbit becomes relevant to law only through conduct, institutional responsibility and a rule applicable to that conduct. The strategic significance of the information thus explains why the problem matters, while legal analysis determines which consequences can be justified, challenged or remedied. 4. Who Acts When the Satellite Is Commercial? Commercial providers complicate legal characterisation because the owner of a spacecraft, the State of registry, the government that licenses operations, the purchaser of imagery and the armed force that eventually uses the product may be different actors. The Outer Space Treaty makes States internationally responsible for national activities in outer space, including those of 8 non-governmental entities, and requires authorisation and continuing supervision under Article VI. Article VIII preserves jurisdiction and control over registered space objects and their personnel in the relevant terms, but jurisdiction over an object should not be mistaken for sovereignty over the Earth territory beneath its orbit. The treaty system therefore creates regulatory responsibilities without collapsing all downstream intelligence transactions into one State act (United Nations, 1967). Responsibility under Article VI also needs to be distinguished from attribution under the general law of State responsibility. The International Law Commission's Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts identify circumstances in which conduct of State organs, entities exercising governmental authority and persons acting on State instructions or under its direction or control can be attributed to a State. Licensing a commercial satellite is not, without more, proof that every delivery of imagery to every customer constitutes the licensing State's own internationally wrongful operation (International Law Commission, 2001). Equally, the commercial form of an activity does not make it immune from accountability where evidence establishes direction, control, adoption or another relevant basis of attribution. The institutional and contractual facts matter as much as the satellite's orbit. A possible allegation of aid or assistance requires similar care. Under Article 16 of the International Law Commission's Articles, responsibility for aid or assistance concerns an internationally wrongful act of another State, the assisting State's knowledge of the circumstances and conduct that would be wrongful if committed by the assisting State itself, subject to the rule's further conditions and its commentary (International Law Commission, 2001). That provision addresses responsibility between States; a private company's supply contract does not, without a legally sufficient connection to a State, satisfy its attribution requirements. Evidence that a 9 company supplied imagery to a defence ministry does not by itself establish the principal wrongful act or the elements of State aid or assistance. Equally, contractual opacity is not conclusive evidence of innocence. Military usefulness, legal attribution and possible complicity remain analytically independent propositions, and each must survive scrutiny on its own facts. This is particularly necessary where information assists a State in exercising a lawful right of defence, because the existence of armed conflict does not render every act supporting one participant wrongful. The inquiry becomes more exacting when intelligence is supplied to an armed force during an international armed conflict. A commercial product can shorten targeting timelines and contribute directly to a particular operation, but it does not follow that every image purchased by a belligerent makes the supplier a combatant or that each State connected to the transaction becomes a party to the conflict. The legal assessment must examine the nature of the assistance, the supplier's conduct and the factual and legal basis for any asserted responsibility, including the circumstances of a concrete attack. For parties bound by Additional Protocol I, Article 52(2) defines military objectives by reference to an object's nature, location, purpose or use, its effective contribution to military action and the definite military advantage offered by its destruction, capture or neutralisation; the core distinction is also reflected in customary humanitarian law. Qualification cannot rest simply on the nationality of the owner or the political identity of a customer (Additional Protocol I, 1977, art. 52(2)). This disaggregation is particularly important for satellites that support both civilian and military services. Navigation, communications and imaging infrastructure can assist armed forces and sustain hospitals, emergency response, agriculture and civilian transport at the same time. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has highlighted the humanitarian consequences 10 of disrupting space services on which essential civilian functions depend (ICRC, 2024). A State contemplating action against such infrastructure must therefore consider the actual military use and the expected civilian effects rather than treating commercial status as absolute protection or military use as blanket permission to attack. The capacity of space technology to serve several purposes makes the factual assessment harder; it does not remove distinction, proportionality and precautions when the law of armed conflict applies. 5. The Contemporary Record: Three Different Forms of Dependence on Orbital Knowledge Recent public announcements illustrate three distinct relationships between orbital observation and State security, although they cannot disclose the classified collection plans or operational decisions that would be necessary for a definitive legal assessment. On the Korean Peninsula, the Republic of Korea reported the completion of its military reconnaissance satellite 425 Project in November 2025, describing improved day-and-night monitoring of North Korean activity (Republic of Korea Ministry of National Defense, 2025). The launch of reconnaissance spacecraft by the Democratic People's Republic of Korea has also been addressed within a separate Security Council framework concerning prohibited ballistic-missile-related activities (United Nations Security Council, 2023). These facts should not be flattened into a claim that collecting an image is unlawful for one side and lawful for the other by reason of political alignment. A restriction concerning a particular launch technology and an allegation concerning the later acquisition of information are legally separate questions. Their coexistence demonstrates why the juridical object of a complaint must be identified with precision. Israel's Ofek 19 offers a different illustration. In September 2025 the Israeli Ministry of Defense stated that the satellite's radar system had returned its first high-resolution images following launch, identifying its role in geospatial intelligence (Israel Ministry of Defense, 2025). 11 The announcement provides credible evidence of a reconnaissance capability and a declared defence purpose. It does not reveal which foreign military facilities were imaged, how the data entered operational planning, whether a particular strike relied on it or whether the relevant legal obligations were respected in any subsequent action. story-92fe53d72a7c521bf2ee154f.content: The world doesn’t operate in layers. It operates under pressure. Defend a coastline. Respond to a flood. Keep the grid running. Less time on screens. More time focused on you. We are proud to launch InterSystems IntelliCare at King’s College Hospital London – Jeddah, led by our Chief Information Officer, Mr. Diaa Kamal, with the support of our Chief Executive Officer, Dr. Ibrahim Alharfi, and in the presence of Prof. Ezzeldin M. Ibrahim, Deputy Chief Medical Officer and Chair of Oncology. story-98f3dafe1a51e93c24eaa367.content: Ukrainian soldiers in the Donetsk region narrowly escaped a Russian FPV drone strike after jumping out of their vehicle just moments before it was hit. The incident highlights how modern warfare is rapidly changing. The Russia-Ukraine war has demonstrated the growing importance of inexpensive FPV drones, real-time battlefield surveillance, electronic warfare and artificial intelligence. Traditional military assets, including tanks and armoured vehicles, are increasingly vulnerable to small, relatively low cost drones. Modern warfare is no longer determined solely by troop numbers, tanks or firepower. Drone technology, intelligence gathering, electronic warfare and the ability to detect and respond to threats in real time are becoming increasingly important in determining battlefield outcomes.

story-9cdff4a7f081959f51f6db5e.content: #البحث_العلمي أنثروبك تحلل 207 آلاف جلسة بحثية: أين ينجح Claude في العلم وأين يتعثر!؟ https://t.co/gBx0sHYrHy نشرت Anthropic في 5 نوفمبر 2026 دراسة عن استخدام العلماء لـ Claude، وهذه خلاصتها: ما الذي درسوه؟ حلل الفريق نحو 207 آلاف جلسة بحثية على Claude و Claude Code بأساليب تحفظ الخصوصية، وصنف كل جلسة بحسب المجال العلمي ونوع المهمة فقط، دون الاحتفاظ بمحتوى الأبحاث نفسها. أين يُستخدم أكثر؟ قياساً بعدد الباحثين في كل مجال، يرتفع الاستخدام في العلوم التطبيقية مثل علوم الحاسب والرياضيات والإحصاء، وينخفض في العلوم الصحية والعلوم المخبرية. مثلاً، علوم الحاسوب تمثل 4.3% فقط من باحثي العالم لكنها تستحوذ على 32.7% من جلسات Claude Code. في أي مهام؟ تحليل البيانات يشكل نحو ثلث الجلسات على Claude وقرابة نصفها على Claude Code، وتليه الكتابة. المفارقة أن توليد الأفكار وجمع البيانات أقل استخداماً، مع أن العلماء في استطلاع مرافق اعتبروهما الأهم للاكتشاف العلمي. أما في أداة Claude Science المتخصصة، فحصة توليد الأفكار تبلغ نحو ضعف نظيرتها على Claude. لماذا هذا التفاوت؟ الخلاصة أن العلماء يستخدمون الذكاء الاصطناعي حيث يعمل جيداً. المهام الأنسب له تحظى باستخدام يفوق المتوقع بمرتين إلى أربع مرات، بينما المهام الأقل ملاءمة، وأغلبها عمل فيزيائي، تكاد لا تُستخدم فيها. ماذا عن المستقبل؟ وضع الباحثون سيناريوهات توضيحية وليست تنبؤات: •لو انتشرت القدرات الحالية على نطاق واسع، قد يتضاعف الإنتاج البحثي في بعض المجالات. •لو أتمت الذكاء الاصطناعي كل العمل غير الفيزيائي، قد يرتفع الإنتاج في مجالات مثل علوم الحاسب والإحصاء حتى 15 ضعفاً، مقابل ثلاثة أو أربعة أضعاف في الكيمياء والأحياء بسبب قيود العمل المخبري. •نحو 40% من الباحثين المستطلَعين يتوقعون أن ينفذ الذكاء الاصطناعي مشاريع بحثية كاملة بمفرده بحلول 2030. تحفظات مهمة تنبه الدراسة إلى أن التبني قد يتأخر كثيراً عن القدرات، وأن تراجع الإشراف البشري قد يفتح الباب لأبحاث خطرة أو غير أخلاقية. كما أن عينة الاستطلاع من متقدمين لمنح Anthropic، فهم على الأرجح أكثر استخداماً للذكاء الاصطناعي من العالِم العادي.

story-9efe3beda197e08facc5d486.content: 🔴 حذر تقرير أصدره معهد دراسات الأمن القومي الإسرائيلي (INSS)، في 17 نوفمبر 2026، من أن التطور المتسارع في التقنيات الكمومية قد يهدد التفوق العسكري النوعي الذي تتمتع به إسرائيل، خصوصاً مع تقدم إيران في هذا المجال واحتمال تطوير تقنيات استشعار ورادارات قادرة مستقبلاً على كشف الطائرات الشبحية والصواريخ والغواصات. واعتبر المعهد أن المنافسة على التفوق الكمومي أصبحت هدفاً استراتيجياً للقوى الكبرى وإسرائيل، وقد تؤدي إلى تحول في طبيعة الحروب تتحدد نتائجه بدرجة متزايدة وفق التفوق التكنولوجي. 🔷 صنف التقرير إيران في المرتبة الأولى على مستوى الشرق الأوسط في مجالات العلوم والتكنولوجيا الكمومية، وهو ما يكتسب أهمية خاصة في ظل المواجهة العسكرية المستمرة مع إسرائيل والولايات المتحدة. ويشير التقييم إلى أن انتشار التقنيات الكمومية مستقبلاً قد يتيح لدول أصغر تطوير قدرات كانت حكراً على القوى المتقدمة، بما يؤثر في التوازن العسكري والاستخباري. 🔷 حدد المعهد تقنيات الاستشعار الكمومي باعتبارها أحد أبرز مصادر التهديد المستقبلي للتفوق العسكري الإسرائيلي. وتشمل التطبيقات المحتملة رادارات أكثر تقدماً في اكتشاف الأهداف منخفضة البصمة، وأجهزة استشعار للصواريخ والغواصات، إلى جانب تطورات في التشفير وتحليل المعلومات الاستخبارية والمحاكاة العسكرية. وإذا بلغت هذه التقنيات مستويات نضج عملياتية كافية، فقد تؤثر في فاعلية بعض مزايا التخفي والاستطلاع الحالية. غير أن هذه التطبيقات لا تزال متفاوتة في درجة نضجها، ولا يمثل التقرير إثباتاً لإمكان استخدامها جميعاً في المدى القريب. 🔷 كشف التقرير عن استثمارات إسرائيلية متزايدة في القطاع الكمومي، مع تصنيفها في المرتبة الثانية عالمياً بعد الصين من حيث الاستثمار نسبة إلى الناتج المحلي الإجمالي، والخامسة من حيث التمويل الإجمالي، والسابعة في الابتكار الكمومي. وأشار إلى أن الشركات الإسرائيلية جمعت نحو 500 مليون دولار خلال عام 2025، بما يعادل 9% من الاستثمار الخاص العالمي في هذا المجال، وفق تقرير لهيئة الابتكار الإسرائيلية ومركز الثورة الصناعية الرابعة. وارتفع عدد الشركات الإسرائيلية العاملة في القطاع من نحو خمس شركات عام 2019 إلى أكثر من عشرين شركة بحلول 2025. 🔷 أطلقت الحكومة الإسرائيلية خلال أكتوبر 2026 مشروعاً وطنياً باسم «نيكسوس»، يهدف إلى تطوير منصة حوسبة كمومية محلية الصنع وتقليص الاعتماد على التقنيات الأجنبية. ويأتي المشروع ضمن توجه لتعزيز السيادة التكنولوجية الإسرائيلية في المجالات التي ترتبط مستقبلاً بالاستخبارات والأمن السيبراني والحوسبة المتقدمة. 🔷 قدم مايكل شتيرن، الباحث في الفيزياء الكمومية بمعهد التخنيون الإسرائيلي، تقديراً بأن الوصول إلى قدرات حوسبة كمومية متقدمة قد يصبح ممكناً خلال خمس إلى عشر سنوات، بعدما كان يعتقد قبل 15 عاماً أنها تحتاج إلى ما بين 50 ومئة عام. وعزا تسارع التطور إلى دخول الذكاء الاصطناعي في تحسين الخوارزميات، وتوليد إشارات التحكم، وأتمتة معايرة البتات الكمومية، ما يقلص الحاجة إلى التدخل البشري في تشغيل الأنظمة المعقدة. 🔷 اعتبر شتيرن أن دمج الذكاء الاصطناعي بالحوسبة الكمومية قد يمثل تحولاً تكنولوجياً يصعب تقدير تداعياته الأمنية والاجتماعية حالياً. وقارن المرحلة الراهنة بالبدايات الأولى للتكنولوجيا النووية، حين سبقت التطبيقات العسكرية الاستخدامات المدنية الواسعة. لكنه أكد أن التقدم العلمي سيستمر، وأن التحدي الأساسي يتعلق بكيفية إدارة المخاطر المصاحبة للتكنولوجيا.

story-9f165ee7d87a167bd2f6d687.content: الجساس مسيرة سعودية بالذكاء الاصطناعي الجساس مسيرة سعودية الصنع 100%، تعتمد بشكل أساسي على الذكاء الاصطناعي في مهام الاستطلاع والدفاع. ظهرت بشكل واضح في ملتقى الصناعات العسكرية، ووصل سرعتها المعلنة إلى 150 كم/ساعة.⁠ هي واحدة من 8 أنواع طائرات بدون طيار ينتجها مصنع دفاع المتحدة في القصيم. المصنع معتمد من الهيئة العامة للصناعات العسكرية (GAMI)، وقدرته الإنتاجية تصل لنحو 300 طائرة سنويًا مع إمكانية مضاعفتها لـ600.⁠ من الشكل الظاهر في التقارير، تبدو الجساس من النوع متعدد الدوارات (multi-rotor)، مناسب لمهام الاستطلاع التكتيكي والقريب، ومزودة بأنظمة تصوير وحساسات تدعم الذكاء الاصطناعي في التعرف على الأهداف والمراقبة. وهي جزء من منظومة "درع" التي تشمل طائرات استطلاع أخرى من نفس المصنع. انتظروا المسيرة القادمة سلطانة 🙂

story-a1da3dfcd6023f861cc77719.content: Your Smart TV is probably showing you ads, recommendations, and apps you never asked for. This free GitHub project can clean all of that up. 😳 Meet CleanYourTV an open-source tool that removes bloatware from Android TV and Google TV over Wi-Fi and replaces the default home screen with a beautiful Apple TV-style launcher. Here's what it does: → Disable manufacturer ads and unwanted recommendations → Remove unnecessary background telemetry → Replace your TV's home screen with a clean, minimalist launcher → Organize your favourite apps into a customizable dock → Customize wallpapers, themes, layouts and app grids → Keep a backup and restore disabled apps whenever you want The interesting part? You don't need to root your TV, connect a cable, or uninstall system apps. It uses Android Debug Bridge (ADB) over Wi-Fi to make the changes. It supports 170+ TV models contributed by the community. Repo: https://t.co/4JWUEMiIB8 Imagine turning that cluttered Smart TV home screen into something that actually feels premium.
