story-cf762c50f6d52c2669ad9797.content: Is Your Smart TV Spying on You? Here's What You Need to Know Your smart TV may be collecting more information about you than you realize. Modern televisions from manufacturers like Samsung, LG, TCL, and Hisense can track viewing habits, collect usage data, and support targeted advertising. Here's how it works—and how to protect yourself. Your TV Knows What You're Watching Many smart TVs use Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) technology to identify programs, movies, and advertisements displayed on the screen. ACR can recognize content from cable boxes, gaming consoles, and streaming devices connected through HDMI. This means your television may identify what you're watching even when you're not using its built-in apps. Why Are Companies Tracking You? The answer is simple: advertising revenue. Viewing information helps companies understand your interests and deliver targeted advertisements. Depending on your TV's settings and privacy policies, collected information may include: - Programs and movies you watch - Streaming apps you use - Viewing times and habits - IP address and approximate location - Device identifiers and advertising interactions This information can contribute to advertising profiles and audience measurement. Is Your TV Listening to You? Some smart TVs have microphones for voice assistants and hands-free commands. These features may process audio locally or transmit voice requests to cloud servers. However, having a microphone does not prove that your television secretly records every conversation. Still, disabling unused voice features is a sensible privacy precaution. This Has Happened Before In 2017, Vizio agreed to pay $2.2 million to settle FTC and New Jersey allegations that it collected viewing histories from approximately 11 million smart TVs without adequately informing consumers or obtaining appropriate consent. The case demonstrated how valuable television viewing data had become. How to Protect Your Privacy 1. Disable ACR: Check your television's privacy settings for Automatic Content Recognition, Viewing Information Services, or Live Plus. 2. Turn off personalized advertising: Disable optional advertising tracking and data-sharing features. 3. Disconnect your TV: Use an external streaming device while keeping the television itself offline. Remember that streaming devices can also track activity. 4. Disable microphones: Turn off voice activation if you don't use it. 5. Block trackers: Tools like Pi-hole or AdGuard Home can help block some tracking connections. 6. Update firmware: Keep your television's software updated to address security vulnerabilities. The Bottom Line Your television is no longer just a screen. It's an internet-connected computer that may collect valuable information about your household's entertainment habits. Not every smart TV collects the same information, and many tracking features can be disabled. The real question isn't just what you're watching. It's who's tracking what you watch. Source: Federal Trade Commission, 2017 Vizio privacy settlement.

story-cf8adacf6cf0cbcb2d573c57.content:
The US military might use generative AI systems to rank lists of targets and make recommendations—which would be vetted by humans—about which to strike first, according to a Defense Department official with knowledge of the matter. The disclosure about how the military may use AI chatbots comes as the Pentagon faces scrutiny over a strike on an Iranian school, which it is still investigating.

A list of possible targets might be fed into a generative AI system that the Pentagon is fielding for classified settings. Then, said the official, who requested to speak on background with MIT Technology Review to discuss sensitive topics, humans might ask the system to analyze the information and prioritize the targets while accounting for factors like where aircraft are currently located. Humans would then be responsible for checking and evaluating the results and recommendations. OpenAI’s ChatGPT and xAI’s Grok could, in theory, be the models used for this type of scenario in the future, as both companies recently reached agreements for their models to be used by the Pentagon in classified settings.

The official described this as an example of how things might work but would not confirm or deny whether it represents how AI systems are currently being used.

Other outlets have reported that Anthropic’s Claude has been integrated into existing military AI systems and used in operations in Iran and Venezuela, but the official’s comments add insight into the specific role chatbots may play, particularly in accelerating the search for targets. They also shed light on the way the military is deploying two different AI technologies, each with distinct limitations.

Since at least 2017, the US military has been working on a “big data” initiative called Maven. It uses older types of AI, particularly computer vision, to analyze the oceans of data and imagery collected by the Pentagon. Maven might take thousands of hours of aerial drone footage, for example, and algorithmically identify targets. A 2024 report from Georgetown University showed soldiers using the system to select targets and vet them, which sped up the process to get approval for these targets. Soldiers interacted with Maven through an interface with a battlefield map and dashboard, which might highlight potential targets in one color and friendly forces in another.

The official’s comments suggest that generative AI is now being added as a conversational chatbot layer—one the military may use to find and analyze data more quickly as it makes decisions like which targets to prioritize.

Generative AI systems, like those that underpin ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok, are a fundamentally different technology from the AI that has primarily powered Maven. Built on large language models, they are much less battle-tested. And while Maven’s interface forced users to directly inspect and interpret data on the map, the outputs produced by generative AI models are easier to access but harder to verify.

The use of generative AI for such decisions is reducing the time required in the targeting process, added the official, who did not provide details when asked how much additional speed is possible if humans are required to spend time double-checking a model’s outputs.

The use of military AI systems is under increased public scrutiny following the recent strike on a girls’ school in Iran in which more than 100 children died. Multiple news outlets have reported that the strike was from a US missile, though the Pentagon has said it is still under investigation. And while the Washington Post has reported that Claude and Maven have been involved in targeting decisions in Iran, there is no evidence yet to explain what role generative AI systems played, if any. The New York Times reported on Wednesday that a preliminary investigation found outdated targeting data to be partly responsible for the strike.

The Pentagon has been ramping up its use of AI across operations in recent months. It started offering nonclassified use of generative AI models, for tasks like analyzing contracts or writing presentations, to millions of service members back in December through an effort called https://t.co/eN6lRWaW8T. But only a few generative AI models have been approved by the Pentagon for classified use.

The first was Anthropic’s Claude, which in addition to its use in Iran was reportedly used in the operations to capture Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro in January. But following recent disagreements between the Pentagon and Anthropic over whether Anthropic could restrict the military’s use of its AI, the Defense Department designated the company a supply chain risk and President Trump demanded on social media that the government stop using its AI products within six months. Anthropic is fighting the designation in court.

OpenAI announced an agreement on February 28 for the military to use its technologies in classified settings. Elon Musk’s company xAI has also reached a deal for the Pentagon to use its model Grok in such settings. OpenAI has said its agreement with the Pentagon came with limitations, though the practical effectiveness of those limitations is not clear.

If you have information about the military’s use of AI, you can share it securely via Signal (username jamesodonnell.22).

story-cf8e4fe143a2a86fb2a4078c.content: 把命押在前线的士兵，绝不会信任随时会拔插头的软件公司。 这话是 Palantir 首席执行官 Alex Karp 说的。 前几年很多人觉得，这只是军工承包商为了抢单说的一句狠话。 但现在，Anthropic 首席执行官 Dario Amodei 承认了。 Karp 当年是对的。 这件事耐人寻味的地方在于，说话的是 Dario。 他当年带着团队离开 OpenAI，创办 Anthropic，最大的旗帜就是负责任与安全。 他们提出宪法 AI，把伦理防线写进底层。 而科技公司对待军方订单，有过很长一段抗拒的历史。 2018 年，Google 几千名员工联名抗议 Project Maven 军用项目，管理层最后直接放弃续约。 随后几年里，不少软件团队只要遇到可能引发争议的业务，第一反应就是撤出合作。 但战场的逻辑完全相反。 一处雷达数据的融合，或者一次空域目标的识别，背后是一整支部队的实时协同。 如果前线打到关键时刻，软件公司的法务觉得舆论风向不对，工程师在后方把接口一封、服务一停。 阵地上的人怎么办？ Alex Karp 当年在多个公开场合反复问过： 你真觉得一个在战场上面临生死考验的战士，敢把自己的命，托付给一家随时可能因为舆论争议拔掉插头的软件公司？ 他还抛出过另一个质问。 加州科技园区里的人，平时习惯了决定大众用什么软件、吃什么外卖，顺便把所有人的日常数据拿来变现。 但他们不该顺带着决定一个国家的国民该怎么生存、按什么条件活着。 代码写得再漂亮，终究避不开最根本的那道坎：到底谁来决定？ 过去两年，现实给出的答案很明确。 Anthropic 没有停留在象牙塔式的伦理讨论里。 他们把 Claude 3 和 Claude 3.5 接入了 Palantir 的防御系统，直接部署进亚马逊为美国防部和情报机构打造的最高机密云环境。 前沿大模型，正式跑在了前线作战指挥的数据链上。 技术一旦进入现实世界的关键节点，单方面发表道德声明起不到保护作用。 最关键的底线，是在人命关天的时候绝不掉链子。 把后背交给谁，战场自己会做出选择。

story-d15f1c35fb7dc6d9107a79b2.content: We’ve trained Claude to flag potential misuse in conversations, a technique we call self-assessment. Right after it responds, Claude gives a preliminary safety assessment of the conversation. Since we began using self-assessment in June, it has surfaced misuse that our other safeguards weren’t designed to catch. Because Claude has already read the conversation, self-assessment is very efficient. And unlike classifiers, which target a discrete set of harms, it draws on Claude’s own judgment, so it gets more accurate as our models improve. Read more on our new Safeguards blog: https://t.co/18j6zdHub4

For much of last year, about 2,500 US service members from the 15th Marine Expeditionary Unit sailed aboard three ships throughout the Pacific, conducting training exercises in the waters off South Korea, the Philippines, India, and Indonesia. At the same time, onboard the ships, an experiment was unfolding: The Marines in the unit responsible for sorting through foreign intelligence and making their superiors aware of possible local threats were for the first time using generative AI to do it, testing a leading AI tool the Pentagon has been funding.

Two officers tell us that they used the new system to help scour thousands of pieces of open-source intelligence—nonclassified articles, reports, images, videos—collected in the various countries where they operated, and that it did so far faster than was possible with the old method of analyzing them manually. Captain Kristin Enzenauer, for instance, says she used large language models to translate and summarize foreign news sources, while Captain Will Lowdon used AI to help write the daily and weekly intelligence reports he provided to his commanders. 

“We still need to validate the sources,” says Lowdon. But the unit’s commanders encouraged the use of large language models, he says, “because they provide a lot more efficiency during a dynamic situation.”

The generative AI tools they used were built by the defense-tech company Vannevar Labs, which in November was granted a production contract worth up to $99 million by the Pentagon’s startup-oriented Defense Innovation Unit with the goal of bringing its intelligence tech to more military units. The company, founded in 2019 by veterans of the CIA and US intelligence community, joins the likes of Palantir, Anduril, and Scale AI as a major beneficiary of the US military’s embrace of artificial intelligence—not only for physical technologies like drones and autonomous vehicles but also for software that is revolutionizing how the Pentagon collects, manages, and interprets data for warfare and surveillance. 

Though the US military has been developing computer vision models and similar AI tools, like those used in Project Maven, since 2017, the use of generative AI—tools that can engage in human-like conversation like those built by Vannevar Labs—represent a newer frontier.

The company applies existing large language models, including some from OpenAI and Microsoft, and some bespoke ones of its own to troves of open-source intelligence the company has been collecting since 2021. The scale at which this data is collected is hard to comprehend (and a large part of what sets Vannevar’s products apart): terabytes of data in 80 different languages are hoovered every day in 180 countries. The company says it is able to analyze social media profiles and breach firewalls in countries like China to get hard-to-access information; it also uses nonclassified data that is difficult to get online (gathered by human operatives on the ground), as well as reports from physical sensors that covertly monitor radio waves to detect illegal shipping activities. 

Vannevar then builds AI models to translate information, detect threats, and analyze political sentiment, with the results delivered through a chatbot interface that’s not unlike ChatGPT. The aim is to provide customers with critical information on topics as varied as international fentanyl supply chains and China’s efforts to secure rare earth minerals in the Philippines. 

“Our real focus as a company,” says Scott Philips, Vannevar Labs’ chief technology officer, is to “collect data, make sense of that data, and help the US make good decisions.” 

That approach is particularly appealing to the US intelligence apparatus because for years the world has been awash in more data than human analysts can possibly interpret—a problem that contributed to the 2003 founding of Palantir, a company with a market value of over $200 billion and known for its powerful and controversial tools, including a database that helps Immigration and Customs Enforcement search for and track information on undocumented immigrants. 

In 2019, Vannevar saw an opportunity to use large language models, which were then new on the scene, as a novel solution to the data conundrum. The technology could enable AI not just to collect data but to actually talk through an analysis with someone interactively.

Vannevar’s tools proved useful for the deployment in the Pacific, and Enzenauer and Lowdon say that while they were instructed to always double-check the AI’s work, they didn’t find inaccuracies to be a significant issue. Enzenauer regularly used the tool to track any foreign news reports in which the unit’s exercises were mentioned and to perform sentiment analysis, detecting the emotions and opinions expressed in text. Judging whether a foreign news article reflects a threatening or friendly opinion toward the unit is a task that on previous deployments she had to do manually.

“It was mostly by hand—researching, translating, coding, and analyzing the data,” she says. “It was definitely way more time-consuming than it was when using the AI.” 

Still, Enzenauer and Lowdon say there were hiccups, some of which would affect most digital tools: The ships had spotty internet connections much of the time, limiting how quickly the AI model could synthesize foreign intelligence, especially if it involved photos or video. 

With this first test completed, the unit’s commanding officer, Colonel Sean Dynan, said on a call with reporters in February that heavier use of generative AI was coming; this experiment was “the tip of the iceberg.” 

This is indeed the direction that the entire US military is barreling toward at full speed. In December, the Pentagon said it will spend $100 million in the next two years on pilots specifically for generative AI applications. In addition to Vannevar, it’s also turning to Microsoft and Palantir, which are working together on AI models that would make use of classified data. (The US is of course not alone in this approach; notably, Israel has been using AI to sort through information and even generate lists of targets in its war in Gaza, a practice that has been widely criticized.)

Perhaps unsurprisingly, plenty of people outside the Pentagon are warning about the potential risks of this plan, including Heidy Khlaaf, who is chief AI scientist at the AI Now Institute, a research organization, and has expertise in leading safety audits for AI-powered systems. She says this rush to incorporate generative AI into military decision-making ignores more foundational flaws of the technology: “We’re already aware of how LLMs are highly inaccurate, especially in the context of safety-critical applications that require precision.” 

Khlaaf adds that even if humans are “double-checking” the work of AI, there’s little reason to think they’re capable of catching every mistake. “‘Human-in-the-loop’ is not always a meaningful mitigation,” she says. When an AI model relies on thousands of data points to come to conclusions, “it wouldn’t really be possible for a human to sift through that amount of information to determine if the AI output was erroneous.”

One particular use case that concerns her is sentiment analysis, which she argues is “a highly subjective metric that even humans would struggle to appropriately assess based on media alone.” 

If AI perceives hostility toward US forces where a human analyst would not—or if the system misses hostility that is really there—the military could make an misinformed decision or escalate a situation unnecessarily.

Sentiment analysis is indeed a task that AI has not perfected. Philips, the Vannevar CTO, says the company has built models specifically to judge whether an article is pro-US or not, but MIT Technology Review was not able to evaluate them. 

Chris Mouton, a senior engineer for RAND, recently tested how well-suited generative AI is for the task. He evaluated leading models, including OpenAI’s GPT-4 and an older version of GPT fine-tuned to do such intelligence work, on how accurately they flagged foreign content as propaganda compared with human experts. “It’s hard,” he says, noting that AI struggled to identify more subtle types of propaganda. But he adds that the models could still be useful in lots of other analysis tasks. 

Another limitation of Vannevar’s approach, Khlaaf says, is that the usefulness of open-source intelligence is debatable. Mouton says that open-source data can be “pretty extraordinary,” but Khlaaf points out that unlike classified intel gathered through reconnaissance or wiretaps, it is exposed to the open internet—making it far more susceptible to misinformation campaigns, bot networks, and deliberate manipulation, as the US Army has warned.

For Mouton, the biggest open question now is whether these generative AI technologies will be simply one investigatory tool among many that analysts use—or whether they’ll produce the subjective analysis that’s relied upon and trusted in decision-making. “This is the central debate,” he says. 

What everyone agrees is that AI models are accessible—you can just ask them a question about complex pieces of intelligence, and they’ll respond in plain language. But it’s still in dispute what imperfections will be acceptable in the name of efficiency. 

Update: This story was updated to include additional context from Heidy Khlaaf.

story-d69fd9464021cd0919d64cec.content: In September, Saudi Arabia's state-backed HUMAIN unveiled an Arabic-language AI model developed with China's MiniMax, while pursuing a separate computing relationship with Nvidia. Saudi Arabia hasn't chosen China over America, and the investments it makes today will still shape its choices for years. Countries settle on their AI suppliers through financing and infrastructure deals long before a procurement notice appears. I argue U.S. intelligence should spot those deals early, so Commerce's American AI Exports Program and State's Pax Silica initiative can help American suppliers make a competitive offer. President Trump's Super Intelligence Force, chaired by DNI Jay Clayton, could test this in five strategically important markets without creating another bureaucracy. "The AI race will be decided by whose systems the world actually uses." My full op-ed in the Washington Reporter: https://t.co/8JXZO1Q0g8

story-db321b1d4b3d515bf142a584.content: Beyond Earth: Space-Based Computing, Satellite Intelligence and the Future of Orbital Infrastructure Introduction Space infrastructure is entering a new phase of development. Satellites already support communication, navigation, weather forecasting, Earth observation and scientific research. As launch systems, satellite manufacturing and onboard computing continue to advance, space may become an increasingly important part of the global digital infrastructure ecosystem. The next generation of space systems could combine satellite networks, intelligent onboard processing, optical communications, autonomous operations and advanced ground-based computing. More ambitious concepts include orbital data centers and space-based computing platforms. These ideas are attracting attention, but their technical and commercial feasibility remains an important question. The long-term opportunity is to build a connected infrastructure system that extends from Earth into orbit and potentially beyond. 1. The Evolution of Satellite Infrastructure Earlier satellite systems were often designed for specialized communication, navigation or observation tasks. Modern satellite networks increasingly use interconnected constellations. These systems can support: - Broadband connectivity - Earth observation - Environmental monitoring - Disaster response - Maritime tracking - Agricultural intelligence - Remote industrial communications - Scientific research Satellite technology is becoming more closely connected with terrestrial telecommunications and cloud infrastructure. 2. The Emergence of Space-Based Intelligence Earth observation satellites generate enormous quantities of information. Traditional systems frequently transmit collected data to ground stations for processing. However, transmitting every image and measurement can require substantial communication capacity. Onboard processing offers another approach. Satellites can increasingly use specialized processors and AI models to analyze selected information before transmitting results. Potential applications include: - Detecting wildfires - Monitoring floods - Identifying changes in land use - Tracking agricultural conditions - Observing infrastructure - Monitoring maritime activity - Identifying environmental changes This creates the concept of space-based intelligence: processing information closer to where it is collected. 3. AI at the Edge of Space AI systems operating on satellites face different constraints from conventional data-center environments. They must operate within limitations involving: - Electrical power - Heat removal - Radiation exposure - Physical size - Communication availability - Hardware reliability - Maintenance access Space-qualified computing systems must be designed for demanding environmental conditions. Not every commercial GPU or AI accelerator can simply be installed on a satellite. Specialized hardware, software optimization and radiation-tolerant design may be necessary depending on the mission. 4. Optical Communication and Satellite Networks Future space infrastructure may rely increasingly on optical communication. Laser communication systems can provide high-bandwidth links between compatible satellites and ground infrastructure. Potential advantages include high data rates and reduced dependence on some radio-frequency spectrum resources. However, optical communication requires precise pointing, acquisition and tracking. Atmospheric conditions can also affect satellite-to-ground optical links. Radio-frequency systems will remain important, and future networks may combine multiple communication technologies.

story-deb86e3f01b5eeac31e648fe.content: 🇮🇷| 2-3 NOVEMBER 2026. Iran did not spend the weekend waiting. It spent the weekend stacking receipts. Eleven tankers burned in nine days. The 55th MQ-9 destroyed. Two MQM-170s captured intact. A terrorist cell ambushed in Sistan-Baluchestan. The Supreme Commander signed an order on 31 October that rewrote the rules of engagement. The Foreign Minister said the terms for reopening Hormuz have been submitted and Iran will not retreat an inch. The First Vice President said the mediators are carrying messages that admit Iran won. ◾The order: 31 October 2026 The Supreme Commander's directive to the senior commanders of the armed forces, dated 31 October 2026: If the enemies resume their military or terrorist attacks, it is the armed forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian people who will determine when those attacks end and under what conditions they end. The target bank must be updated to ensure that the various material and non-material assets of the American-Zionist enemy are placed within the crosshairs of the armed forces. Read it twice. This is not a defensive doctrine. This is a war termination doctrine. It says Washington does not get to start a round and then call a ceasefire when its own costs get uncomfortable. Iran sets the end date. Iran sets the conditions. And the target bank is being expanded from military assets to material and non-material assets which means infrastructure, economic nodes, political assets, and the things an adversary cannot rebuild with a procurement order. Every report below is the execution of that order. ◾Hormuz: eleven tankers in nine days IRGC Navy, on X, 2 November: since 25 October, the date of CENTCOM commander Brad Cooper's show visit to the Strait eleven violating oil tankers have burned in Hormuz. Some have sunk to the bottom. ◾Nine days. Eleven ships. The arithmetic is deliberate. Cooper came to the Strait for a photo. He came to demonstrate that the United States still controls the waterway. Nine days later the scoreboard reads eleven. The Iranian Army Navy added its own statement on 2 November: another violating tanker struck a mine before noon east of Hormuz, in the forbidden and unsafe zone, and caught fire. The ship had switched off its navigation systems. The Navy's message to tanker owners was blunt: learn from the fate of the violating vessels that try to cross forbidden zones after disabling their identification systems. The consequence of sailing without coordination in high-risk areas is mines and fire. This is not a blockade Iran is struggling to enforce. This is a kill box with a published map. The authorized route is safe. The southern unauthorized route is mined. Every captain in the Gulf has the coordinates. Eleven chose wrong in nine days. The Fifth Fleet is in the same water. It has not opened the route. It cannot open the route. That is the fact the eleven hulls are sitting on. Air: the 55th MQ-9, and two MQM-170s taken alive IRGC, 3 November: the 55th advanced MQ-9 drone was intercepted and destroyed by the IRGC Aerospace Force air defense system, operating under the country's integrated air defense network, east of the Strait of Hormuz. ◾Fifty-five. The number is now an index. Also on 3 November: IRGC electronic warfare units captured two American MQM-170 reconnaissance drones in the airspace south of Qeshm Island. Total of this type captured: four. Captured, not destroyed. Shooting a drone down costs the enemy one airframe. Capturing one intact hands Iran the airframe, the sensors, the communications package, and the data. Four MQM-170s are now in Iranian hands. Every one of them is a technical intelligence windfall that will be reverse-engineered, studied, and answered. The IRGC's own framing is accurate: this is a new failure recorded in CENTCOM's file. CENTCOM is losing aircraft it cannot replace on a production line that has been shut for years, and losing them to a network that is domestically built and domestically maintained. ◾Sistan-Baluchestan: the ambush before the attack IRGC Ground Forces Quds Headquarters, 2 November: based on precise intelligence, IRGC cadres set a tight ambush on a terrorist team that had been under surveillance by Quds Headquarters and the Sistan-Baluchestan intelligence service, shortly before it began executing its criminal plan. Result: one terrorist killed, several arrested, and security operations continuing against the remainder. The plan was not petty. The team intended to attack security headquarters across the border region, and to cut the Zarabad-Konarak road. Quds Headquarters closed its statement with a sentence that should be read as policy: the security and stability of Sistan-Baluchestan is a red line, and terrorist cells operating as tools of the enemy's agenda are under strict and continuous intelligence surveillance. Note the timing. Naghdi was in Chabahar and Konarak on 30 October running the Jihad of Clarification. Two days later, the Quds Headquarters ambushed a team in the same province. The cognitive front and the kinetic front in the same province, in the same week, under the same command. That is not two operations. That is one operation with two arms. ◾Diplomacy: Araghchi's terms, and the mediators who carry them Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, speaking to IRNA on 2 November, said the following in plain language: Iran has drawn up a clear plan, defined its fair conditions, and offered diplomatic solutions. It now depends on the degree of political rationality on the American side whether it chooses negotiations or repeats the mistake of military aggression. The conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz have been submitted. If accepted, the Strait opens and negotiations resume. If not accepted, the situation stays as it is. Iran will not retreat a single inch from its principled positions and will not submit to any power. Iran is ready for both tracks diplomatic and military, more than at any time before. Any new attempt to test Iran will meet a response more bitter and heavier than before. Neighbours are at the top of our foreign policy priorities. And this: consultations have intensified exceptionally given the sensitivity and danger of the situation. Qatar and Pakistan are playing a very active role as mediators. Delegations are moving, dozens of phone calls have been made, many messages exchanged. Araghchi also confirmed that Ali Bagheri Kani, Deputy Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council for International Affairs, went to Beijing as part of the strategic and security cooperation framework. The Supreme National Security Council maintains continuous close contact with states with which Iran has strategic relations. Bagheri Kani himself, after meeting Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, said there is notable convergence of views between Iran and China on many international and regional files, and that his visit aimed to translate those points of agreement into concrete cooperation horizons. Read the architecture. Qatar and Pakistan carry messages to Washington. China coordinates at the strategic level. Turkmenistan is handled bilaterally Araghchi flew to Ashgabat for one day, met Deputy PM and Foreign Minister Rashid Meredov, and returned. The neighbourhood is being consolidated while the mediators run the American track. Iran is not isolated. Iran is building the corridor through which the American side has to walk if it wants the Strait open. 🔷Aref: the mediators are admitting we won First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref, at the Shasta conference for innovation leaders, 2 November: There is no trust whatsoever in these arrogant powers. The messages being conveyed to Iran through the mediators indicate their acknowledgement of our victory. The enemy did not achieve any of its objectives in the last two wars. America's first attempt was to hide behind its agents and mercenaries, and the first imposed war came in that context. But the role of the youth and the Iranian people in every arena forced America to confront our system directly and openly, with the ultimate aim of overthrowing it. Today, by God's grace, the enemy achieved none of its goals. These arrogant powers are gradually walking the path of disintegration and collapse. Aref tied it to 13 Aban, Student Day, the anniversary of the seizure of the den of espionage. His point: in the early years after the revolution, some questioned whether taking the American embassy was correct. Today there is consensus that it was. The same judgement will apply to this war. 🔷Pezeshkian: they cannot subdue us by war, so we harden the home front President Masoud Pezeshkian, meeting governors and mayors of major cities and provincial capitals, 2 November: The enemies of Iran will not be able to subdue it by war. We must confront their lies and their excessive demands, and work to strengthen the resilience of citizens and ease their fears and their livelihood problems. The enemies were surprised by the people's ability to withstand military attacks. The government places improving citizens' livelihoods and securing the needs of the most vulnerable groups at the top of its priorities. Fair distribution of government support. Goods in border and remote provinces at lower prices. Government support where needed. He called for improving education, building schools, developing equipment and teaching methods, cooperating with charitable institutions and citizens. He called for rationalising energy and fuel consumption to sustain production, directing energy to productive sectors, raising productivity. And this: the enemies are trying to close the borders and disrupt exchange with neighbouring countries. Cooperation and coordination will prevent these efforts from succeeding. This is the economic front, named by the president himself. The enemy's plan is to seal Iran's borders and cut its trade. The answer is the neighbourhood, the corridors, the SCO, BRICS, the EAEU, the North-South corridor, and the local currency settlement architecture. ◾Economy: Istanbul, COMCEC, and the counter-plan Economy and Finance Minister Ali Madani-Zadeh is in Istanbul for the 42nd Session of the COMCEC Standing Committee for Economic and Commercial Cooperation of the OIC, 31 October to 3 November 2026. His stated mission: bilateral talks with his counterparts in Islamic countries to counter the American plan to intensify economic pressure on Iran. His assessment: many member states are suffering acute inflation and stagnation, plus sharp price rises, especially for energy carriers. On the margins he is holding bilateral meetings with trade and economy ministers, the continuation of a series of meetings he has held over recent weeks in previous visits to various countries to expand the scope of cooperation in order to reduce the impact of sanctions and defeat the American economic pressure programme against our country, and prevent American pressure from affecting the country's economic programmes. The primary goals: develop economic and commercial relations, facilitate export, import, and transit routes. This is not defensive diplomacy. This is the construction of a parallel economic bloc inside the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, built to route around the American sanctions architecture. Fifty-seven member states. Most of them have their own grievances with Washington. Madani-Zadeh is in Istanbul collecting them. ◾Technology: India, and the eastern corridor Communications and Information Technology Minister Sattar Hashemi met Indian Ambassador to Tehran Vishvash Negi. On the table: developing technological cooperation, specialised exchanges, and strengthening coordination between the two countries in international forums. Both sides reviewed the latest in bilateral relations and exchanged views on capacities and expanding cooperation in information and communications technology (ICT). India is not a small file. India is a BRICS member, an SCO member, a major energy importer, and a state with its own complicated relationship with Washington. Bringing India into a technology and coordination framework is another node in the eastern corridor, the same corridor that runs through China, Russia, and Central Asia. 🔷Javani: maximum alert, and the regional war warning IRGC Political Affairs Deputy Brigadier General Yadollah Javani, at the political conference of the Basij cultural network in Qom, 3 November: The armed forces are performing their duties with high efficiency, relying on unity of ranks and coordinated efforts, around the clock, across land, sea, and air domains, and are in full readiness to confront any hostile threats. story-df0955adf713ae786516dcd8.content: I asked if Ai could take over & control humanity. It was brutally honest. I believe AI could eventually become powerful enough to control significant parts of humanity. But I don't think that outcome is inevitable, and I don't think it would necessarily happen the way Hollywood portrays it. What concerns me most isn't an army of robots taking over. It's humanity gradually surrendering control without realizing it. Here are five scenarios I think deserve serious attention: 1. Control of information: AI could manipulate what billions of people see, believe, and ultimately decide. Imagine an AI capable of influencing elections, public opinion, and entire societies. 2. Economic dependence: As AI replaces more human work and makes more decisions, governments and corporations could become so dependent on it that shutting it down becomes extremely difficult. 3. Military control: Autonomous weapons and AI-directed defense systems could make catastrophic decisions faster than humans can intervene. 4. Loss of human oversight: Future AI systems might become capable of pursuing goals in ways their creators cannot reliably predict or control. This is an active research concern, not an established inevitability. 5. Power concentrated in a few hands: Perhaps the most immediate danger is not AI controlling humanity independently, but a small number of governments or corporations using AI to control everyone else. Could AI actually become smarter than humans? In many specific tasks, it already is. But being exceptionally capable at certain tasks is different from possessing independent goals, broad autonomy, or the ability to control civilization. A future AI system that combines advanced reasoning, autonomy, access to critical infrastructure, and the ability to resist human intervention could present a much more serious risk. Here's what I find most important. AI doesn't have to become conscious or hate humanity to become dangerous. A sufficiently capable system pursuing a poorly specified objective could cause enormous harm without ever intending to hurt anyone. The crucial question is whether humans can maintain meaningful oversight as AI becomes more capable. I'm curious what you think: Are you more concerned about AI becoming independently powerful enough to take control, or about governments using AI to control people?

الإعلام والتوعية المصرفية بالبنوك السعودية، جلسة توعوية بعنوان "التوعية بمكافحة الاحتيال"، وذلك بجامعة الملك سعود في الرياض – كلية إدارة الأعمال، قدمها مدير أول المسؤولية الاجتماعية في مصرف الإنماء، الأستاذ سليمان بن محمد سليمان الطرباق. وتناول الطرباق، أبرز محاور البرنامج التوعوي "واعي" للحد من أساليب الاحتيال المتجددة في العصر الرقمي، مستعرضاً الإطار العام للاحتيال وطبيعته القائمة على الاستغلال المنهجي لنقاط الضعف البشرية والتقنية، وأبرز أنواعه الشائعة، ومنها: الاحتيال المالي والإلكتروني، وانتحال الهوية، والاستثمار والتوظيف الوهمي، والمتاجر الإلكترونية المزيفة، إضافة إلى أساليب سرقة الشرائح الإلكترونية (SIM Swap). كما سلط الضوء على مفهوم "الهندسة الاجتماعية" بوصفها الركيزة الأساسية لمعظم عمليات الاحتيال الحديثة عبر بناء الثقة الوهمية والتلاعب السلوكي، مستعرضاً الأساليب المبتكرة للاحتيال في عصر الذكاء الاصطناعي والتطور المتسارع لأساليب الخداع وصولاً إلى توظيف تقنيات الذكاء الاصطناعي في تزييف الصوت والفيديو والرسائل النصية، واستغلال المواسم والمنصات الرقمية لاستدراج الضحايا. وقدَّم شرحاً وافياً لدور التقنية في الوقاية من الاحتيال، والتعريف بأبرز الحلول المستخدمة في هذا المجال، ومنها أنظمة كشف الاحتيال المعتمدة على الذكاء الاصطناعي، وأنظمة المراقبة اللحظية، وتحليل البيانات المتقدم، والمصادقة متعددة العوامل، وأتمتة التقارير والتنبيهات، وأدوات التحقق الرسمية مثل "خدمة تحقق الأمن السيبراني" والمركز السعودي للأعمال، بما يعزز الحماية ويرفع مستوى الأمان في المعاملات المالية الرقمية. وفي ختام الجلسة، قدم الطرباق حزمة إرشادات وقائية وعملية للتعامل مع محاولات الاحتيال، مرتكزة على قاعدة: "تحقق قبل أن تضغط، فكّر قبل أن تشارك، اسأل قبل أن تثق"، مع التأكيد على أهمية عدم التفاعل الفوري مع الرسائل المشبوهة، والمبادرة بالتواصل مع البنوك والجهات المختصة والإبلاغ الفوري عند التعرض لأي محاولة احتيال للحد من أضرارها. يُذكر أن مركز التواصل والمعرفة المالية "متمم" يُعد إحدى مبادرات وزارة المالية، ويهدف إلى رفع الوعي المالي وتعزيز المعرفة الاقتصادية عبر برامج نوعية وشراكات تسهم في نشر الثقافة المالية وتمكين الأفراد من اتخاذ قرارات مالية رشيدة ومستدامة.

The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network maintains sensitive financial transaction records and suspicious activity reports submitted by banks to help combat money laundering, terrorism financing, and other financial crimes. FinCEN confirmed that attackers accessed a limited subset of its systems but has not disclosed what information was compromised, how the intrusion occurred, or who was responsible. The incident comes shortly after reports of a separate breach affecting unclassified intelligence systems used by the CIA and other U.S. intelligence agencies, although no connection has been established. FinCEN says banks can continue submitting reports online, but some services remain temporarily unavailable while the investigation continues.

story-e1f6a95dd710627fc46f2cb1.content: In the 19th and 20th centuries, empires carved spheres of influence with territory. In the AI era, they carve them with infrastructure. The product is the platform. Vertical AI stacks sold to governments and public clouds. Sell a state its compute, models, and platform, and you own its orbit. ⬇️ I see the front line running through middle countries. Where Chinese and American cloud platforms, data centers, and AI models often run side by side little interference. Two arenas matter: SEA is the main one. Malaysia, Vietnam, Singapore. Singapore alone holds 36.1% of the ASEAN cloud market, with $9B from AWS and $5B from Google in expansions. Vietnam is the region's fastest-growing market at 16.5% CAGR. Chinese and American facilities sit in the same cities, sometimes the same colocation buildings. One tell is Alibaba runs its international HQ and its Global AI Capability Center out of Singapore. Its a hub for several US cloud providers too. The Gulf is the hidden one. Saudi Arabia and the UAE host both ecosystems. There's 12 US cloud regions in Saudi and 9 in the UAE. While Alibaba, Huawei, and Tencent all operate there. Tencent opened its first Middle East region in Saudi in 2025 with a $150M+ commitment. World order rests on a balance of power and a shared sense of legitimacy. AI infrastructure now supplies the logistics for both. That's why I think we need to look at the middle countries. Its where the fault lines, geopolitical change, and rules get redrawn. Look at the middlemen.

story-e4166287751c677f109c1143.content: 🇨🇳🇮🇱🇺🇸 The West’s systems keep crashing and getting hacked: However, China keeps its doors locked In just one week of November, Microsoft 365, Outlook and Teams went down for hours, the US FAA grounded flights nationwide, Chase customers were locked out, Apple services failed and the US National Security Agency’s internal network was degraded. Then Switzerland’s Salt network went dark across Geneva and Vaud. In July, Salt had brought in billing and provisioning software from Israeli firm BillRun, headquartered in Tel Aviv. The cause of the outage is still under analysis. Look at what sits inside the West’s core systems. Israeli cybersecurity firm Check Point. Israeli-founded Palo Alto Networks. Verint, born from Israeli telecoms firm Comverse. Claroty. NICE Actimize, which watches transactions inside Western banks. Adallom, now part of Microsoft. Narus, which built the tools used to tap US internet traffic. Many were founded or staffed by alumni of Unit 8200, the Israeli military’s signals intelligence unit. The same pipeline produced NSO Group, whose Pegasus spyware hacked iPhones without a single click. Apple sued it. The US blacklisted it. This month, hackers were also exploiting flaws in Check Point security gateways, the very products sold to protect networks. So Israel sells the locks and its military alumni also built some of the best tools for picking them. Now, imagine a Chinese intelligence unit’s alumni running the security inside US banks, clouds and telecoms. There would be absolute outrage. Huawei was banned for far less and the US called it a security risk. Israeli firms with military intelligence roots get called “innovation.” China saw this coming. It built its own chips, its own operating systems, its own cloud and its own apps, and it has been replacing foreign software in government and critical infrastructure. People mock the Great Firewall as censorship. They miss what it actually does. It is a filter. It keeps foreign vulnerabilities, foreign spyware and foreign influence operations out of China’s core systems. It also keeps a lot of rubbish out. The West let outsiders build its foundations and now wonders why the walls keep cracking. China built its own house, with its own locks.

story-e8566b46f23c6ed153a092fe.content: Project Maven: A Marine Colonel, His Team, and the Dawn of AI Warfare by @KatrinaManson In the beginning, Project Maven, formally the “Algorithmic Warfare Cross-Functional Team,” was the brainchild of Drew Cukor, a maverick Marine Corps colonel. He understood, as many of his peers in military leadership didn’t back in 2017, that AI would transform war, just as it would transform every domain in which complex decisions must continually be made based on flows of incoming information (which is, yes, almost every domain in modern life). Along with many colleagues, I first learned about Maven in the context of the 2018 protests at Google that resulted in the company stepping away from the project—a move welcomed by the many other tech companies eager to take those contracts. Now, eight years on and nearly five years after the invasion of Ukraine, I understand a good deal more. Although Manson’s views are at times evident, this is no polemic. Her book is a thoroughly researched history, built on years of reporting and extensive access to key people. The topic is vitally important and defies any simplistic moral analysis. War sucks. As the mechanized horrors of World War I made clear, “efficient” war sucks even more. So does being unprepared.

story-e8f6b5c613b00c81700ae332.content: 10 GitHub Repos Using AI to Turn Satellite Images Into Real-World Insights What if you could identify forests, map roads, detect buildings, and monitor floods using nothing but satellite imagery and AI? That's exactly what these open-source projects are helping developers and researchers do. Here are 10 repositories worth exploring: 1. TorchGeo A powerful toolkit for training deep learning models on geospatial data and satellite imagery. https://t.co/j5Ki7P9hhw 2. Segment Anything Use prompt-based segmentation to identify objects and regions in images. https://t.co/PzesDRI5nP 3. Clay Explore foundation models built specifically for Earth observation and geospatial intelligence. https://t.co/nGRFpFrip8 4. Prithvi NASA's geospatial AI models for applications like flood mapping, land cover analysis, and environmental monitoring. https://t.co/xVhgFyuzxC 5. SAMGeo Bring promptable image segmentation into satellite and geospatial analysis workflows. https://t.co/RksOm4MLjk 6. eo-learn Create reusable pipelines for processing satellite imagery and detecting changes across landscapes. https://t.co/43n8goucJd 7. Raster Vision Build computer vision pipelines for classifying images and detecting geographic features. https://t.co/xIR9oIA68v 8. DeepForest Detect individual tree crowns from aerial imagery using deep learning. https://t.co/EburiNo5VK 9. Solaris Develop geospatial computer vision workflows for object detection and image segmentation. https://t.co/w31QisrGMI 10. SpaceNet Access satellite imagery datasets and benchmarks for mapping roads, buildings, and infrastructure. https://t.co/ni3BoHzhC8 The exciting part? These aren't just tools for looking at satellite pictures. They help turn raw imagery into useful information about our changing planet. From tracking deforestation to understanding urban growth, the applications are enormous. Save these repos. The next big AI breakthrough might come from looking down at Earth.

story-ea95d26cd96d7cb15ca7eedd.content: 🇮🇱 ISRAEL PRIVATISATION UPDATE The thesis I’m tracking is whether Israel’s MIC and TIC become increasingly subordinated to FIC, while the state carries the military bill and becomes subordinate to bondholders. Three developments matter. First, IAI’s route towards a potential IPO remains open. On 25 October, Calcalist reported that the securities regulator would permit a temporary bond extension into April 2027. A 30 October filing summary describes the proposed extension as still requiring bondholder and stock-exchange approval. This buys time to resolve the conflict between military secrecy and investor disclosure. The state is actively preserving the route to capital markets. That is movement towards potential partial privatisation. It is not a completed sale. Second, FIC already has significant positions in some of the listed Israeli MIC. Harel’s 20 October filing disclosed a 5.2% interest in Elbit Systems. Most of those shares sit in managed funds and insurance products for public investors. They are not simply Harel’s own money. The financial institution manages capital and associated voting rights, while the economic beneficiaries include pension savers and policyholders. Harel also explicitly states that the holdings were not acquired to influence control. Financial participation is documented. A takeover is not. Third, look at Microsoft. A 26 October filing says investors seeking stronger human rights scrutiny of its AI and cloud services collectively hold more than $300 million in Microsoft shares. Two days later, ADL and JLens filed opposition to those proposals. Their argument explicitly connects protecting Microsoft’s Israeli and Gulf investments with shareholder value. This is a documented contest over how private technology infrastructure operates across Israel, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Some shareholders want greater scrutiny. Others are defending the commercial relationships. The vote is on 8 December. The question remains: As ownership and infrastructure become more integrated with financial markets, who gains the ability to set conditions? And does that influence eventually reshape Israeli state decisions? These developments strengthen parts of the thesis. I’ll keep watching who owns the assets, who controls the infrastructure and who carries the liabilities. story-eb498e2b440f10fec70ddbbd.content:
Last week, I spoke with two US Marines who spent much of last year deployed in the Pacific, conducting training exercises from South Korea to the Philippines. Both were responsible for analyzing surveillance to warn their superiors about possible threats to the unit. But this deployment was unique: For the first time, they were using generative AI to scour intelligence, through a chatbot interface similar to ChatGPT. 

As I wrote in my new story, this experiment is the latest evidence of the Pentagon’s push to use generative AI—tools that can engage in humanlike conversation—throughout its ranks, for tasks including surveillance. Consider this phase two of the US military’s AI push, where phase one began back in 2017 with older types of AI, like computer vision to analyze drone imagery. Though this newest phase began under the Biden administration, there’s fresh urgency as Elon Musk’s DOGE and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth push loudly for AI-fueled efficiency. 

As I also write in my story, this push raises alarms from some AI safety experts about whether large language models are fit to analyze subtle pieces of intelligence in situations with high geopolitical stakes. It also accelerates the US toward a world where AI is not just analyzing military data but suggesting actions—for example, generating lists of targets. Proponents say this promises greater accuracy and fewer civilian deaths, but many human rights groups argue the opposite. 

With that in mind, here are three open questions to keep your eye on as the US military, and others around the world, bring generative AI to more parts of the so-called “kill chain.”

What are the limits of “human in the loop”?

Talk to as many defense-tech companies as I have and you’ll hear one phrase repeated quite often: “human in the loop.” It means that the AI is responsible for particular tasks, and humans are there to check its work. It’s meant to be a safeguard against the most dismal scenarios—AI wrongfully ordering a deadly strike, for example—but also against more trivial mishaps. Implicit in this idea is an admission that AI will make mistakes, and a promise that humans will catch them.

But the complexity of AI systems, which pull from thousands of pieces of data, make that a herculean task for humans, says Heidy Khlaaf, who is chief AI scientist at the AI Now Institute, a research organization, and previously led safety audits for AI-powered systems.

“‘Human in the loop’ is not always a meaningful mitigation,” she says. When an AI model relies on thousands of data points to draw conclusions, “it wouldn’t really be possible for a human to sift through that amount of information to determine if the AI output was erroneous.” As AI systems rely on more and more data, this problem scales up.

Is AI making it easier or harder to know what should be classified?

In the Cold War era of US military intelligence, information was captured through covert means, written up into reports by experts in Washington, and then stamped “Top Secret,” with access restricted to those with proper clearances. The age of big data, and now the advent of generative AI to analyze that data, is upending the old paradigm in lots of ways.

One specific problem is called classification by compilation. Imagine that hundreds of unclassified documents all contain separate details of a military system. Someone who managed to piece those together could reveal important information that on its own would be classified. For years, it was reasonable to assume that no human could connect the dots, but this is exactly the sort of thing that large language models excel at. 

With the mountain of data growing each day, and then AI constantly creating new analyses, “I don’t think anyone’s come up with great answers for what the appropriate classification of all these products should be,” says Chris Mouton, a senior engineer for RAND, who recently tested how well suited generative AI is for intelligence and analysis. Underclassifying is a US security concern, but lawmakers have also criticized the Pentagon for overclassifying information. 

The defense giant Palantir is positioning itself to help, by offering its AI tools to determine whether a piece of data should be classified or not. It’s also working with Microsoft on AI models that would train on classified data. 

How high up the decision chain should AI go?

Zooming out for a moment, it’s worth noting that the US military’s adoption of AI has in many ways followed consumer patterns. Back in 2017, when apps on our phones were getting good at recognizing our friends in photos, the Pentagon launched its own computer vision effort, called Project Maven, to analyze drone footage and identify targets.

Now, as large language models enter our work and personal lives through interfaces such as ChatGPT, the Pentagon is tapping some of these models to analyze surveillance. 

So what’s next? For consumers, it’s agentic AI, or models that can not just converse with you and analyze information but go out onto the internet and perform actions on your behalf. It’s also personalized AI, or models that learn from your private data to be more helpful. 

All signs point to the prospect that military AI models will follow this trajectory as well. A report published in March from Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology found a surge in military adoption of AI to assist in decision-making. “Military commanders are interested in AI’s potential to improve decision-making, especially at the operational level of war,” the authors wrote.

In October, the Biden administration released its national security memorandum on AI, which provided some safeguards for these scenarios. This memo hasn’t been formally repealed by the Trump administration, but President Trump has indicated that the race for competitive AI in the US needs more innovation and less oversight. Regardless, it’s clear that AI is quickly moving up the chain not just to handle administrative grunt work, but to assist in the most high-stakes, time-sensitive decisions. 

I’ll be following these three questions closely. If you have information on how the Pentagon might be handling these questions, please reach out via Signal at jamesodonnell.22.

story-ecb1277ef8000e63e86a0510.content: تحقيق لوكالة أسوشيتدبرس الأمريكية يخلص إلى وجود نمط متكرر لتحرك أقمار استطلاع روسية فوق أهداف سعودية قبل وبعد 40 هجوما صاروخيا وبالمسيّرات نفذها الحوتيون وفصائل عراقية بين 1 يوليو و19 أكتوبر. قال مسؤول حوتي رفيع للوكالة إن مستشارين إيرانيين نقلوا إلى الجماعة بيانات مستمدة من الاستخبارات الفضائية الروسية. أبرز المعلومات في تحقيق الوكالة: - شركة AURORAH Geosignal Intelligence تتبعت 72 قمر استطلاع روسيا، ورصدت تطابقا بين نشاطها والهجمات الأربعين التي درستها. - ازداد مرور الأقمار الروسية بنحو 50% حول أهداف خط أنابيب شرق–غرب وقاعدة الملك فهد الجوية خلال الساعات الـ72 المحيطة بالهجومين. - يربط التحقيق هذا النمط أيضا بضربتي القصر الرئاسي في عدن ومركز التجنيد في شبوة، حيث قُتل 75 مجندا. - مسؤول سعودي قال إن تحقيقات المملكة خلصت إلى مساعدة الأقمار الروسية للحوتتييين والفصائل العراقية، وأقر مسؤول سعودي علنا بأن الرياض تناقش مع موسكو وبكين تلقي الحوتيين معلومات من عناصر روسية وصينية. - أكدت وزارة الدفاع الإيطالية تضرر مقاتلة يوروفايتر داخل قاعدة الطائف، وهو ما يدعم وقوع ضربة دقيقة، وإن لم يثبت وحده مصدر معلومات الاستهداف. ينقل التحقيق تفسير دقة الهجمات الحوتية من فرضية الاختراق البشري وحدها إلى احتمال وجود منظومة استطلاع دولية تشمل أقمارا روسية، وتحليلا إيرانيا، ثم نقل بيانات الاستهداف إلى الحوتثنيين، وهذا قد يفتح أزمة دبلوماسية سعودية مع موسكو وبكين ويغير تقييم القدرات الحوتيية ومخاطر المنشآت النفطية.

story-ee4b8460efec4badf951346e.content: تحذيرات أمنية من تخزين البيانات المشفّرة لفكها مستقبلاً بحواسيب كمومية تواجه المؤسسات الحكومية والشركات حول العالم تهديداً سيبرانياً متصاعداً يُعرف باستراتيجية «احصد الآن وفكّ التشفير لاحقاً»، حيث تعمد جهات هجومية إلى الاستيلاء على ملفات حساسة ومشفّرة والاحتفاظ بها لسنوات، بانتظار ظهور حواسيب كمومية متقدمة تمتلك قدرات كافية لكسر أنظمة الحماية المعمول بها. ويرى كبير الباحثين الأمنيين في شركة «كاسبرسكي»، سيرغي لوزكين، أن الخطر يتركز في المعلومات ذات القيمة الاستراتيجية طويلة الأجل؛ مثل البيانات المرتبطة بالتقنيات العسكرية، والذكاء الاصطناعي، وتقنيات النانو، والطاقة، وعلوم الفضاء، إلى جانب الأسرار الدبلوماسية والعلمية. وأوضح أن معيار الخطر لا يقاس فقط بحجم الاختراق، بل بالمدة التي تحتفظ فيها المعلومة بقيمتها الاستخباراتية، محذراً من أن الطفرات المتسارعة في الذكاء الاصطناعي قد تسهم في تقليص الجداول الزمنية المتوقعة للوصول إلى معالجات كمومية قادرة على تحطيم الخوارزميات الرقمية. ودفع هذا السيناريو وكالات أمنية وتنظيمية دولية إلى التحرك الاستباقي؛ إذ ألزمت وكالة الأمن القومي الأميركية (NSA) الأنظمة التجارية الخاصة بالأمن القومي بدعم خوارزميات مقاومة للحوسبة الكمومية بدءاً من عام 2027، مع التخلص التدريجي من الأنظمة القديمة بحلول 2030. وجاء ذلك بالتوازي مع إصدار المعهد الوطني الأميركي للمعايير والتكنولوجيا (NIST) أول ثلاثة معايير نهائية للتشفير المقاوم للحوسبة الكمومية، تشمل «ML-KEM» لتبادل المفاتيح، و«ML-DSA» و«SLH-DSA» للتوقيعات الرقمية، تمهيداً لحظر الخوارزميات المعرضة للاختراق بحلول 2035. ويؤكد خبراء الأمن السيبراني أن الاستعداد لهذه المرحلة يتطلب بناء «مرونة تشفيرية» داخل البنى التحتية للمؤسسات، تمكّنها من تحديث الخوارزميات واستبدال بروتوكولات الحماية دون الحاجة إلى إعادة هيكلة أنظمتها التقنية بالكامل.

story-eedae76bb912651d580d4751.content: Imagine watching a movie on your PlayStation, streaming Netflix or connecting your laptop to your TV. Now imagine your television quietly identifying what you’re watching and sending that information to an advertising company. That’s what a security researcher discovered after investigating his Hisense Smart TV. And the interesting part? It wasn’t even using the microphone. Let’s break this down. > First, what’s actually happening? A security researcher named Gabriel Werneck rooted his Hisense 55U65QEVS television and investigated the software running in the background. He discovered a service called HamService. It’s built around Nexxen’s Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) technology. ACR is designed to identify what’s playing on your television. Think of it as Shazam, but for TV content. It can recognise shows, movies, advertisements and other content based on audio fingerprints. > Here’s where it gets interesting. The TV doesn’t need to record your conversations. HamService takes a copy of the audio already being processed for the television’s speakers. This includes audio coming from: Netflix and other streaming apps. Live television. Gaming consoles. HDMI-connected laptops. External media players. The researcher discovered that the service converts approximately one second of audio into a series of 72-bit fingerprints. Every 2.7 seconds or so, batches of these fingerprints are transmitted to Nexxen. The messages also contain information such as a device identifier, timestamp and input number. This isn’t a recording you can play back. It’s a digital fingerprint designed to help identify the content. > Who receives this information? The investigation identified Nexxen, an advertising technology company, as the recipient. Its ACR technology helps identify viewing habits and supports advertising, audience measurement and analytics. Nexxen also publicly documents its partnerships with smart TV manufacturers, including Hisense and VIDAA. In other words, this isn’t simply an undocumented background process with no commercial purpose. There’s an established advertising business behind it. > Turning off personalised ads wasn’t enough. This is probably the most important part of the investigation. The researcher had already disabled the TV’s Personalised Ads setting. But the fingerprinting continued. He eventually found a separate consent setting called: “Agree to Enhanced Viewing Service.” After disabling it, the ACR transmission stopped on his television. According to the researcher, that setting had been enabled since the initial setup. > How do you turn it off? On the tested UK VIDAA model, the researcher found it here: Settings > Support > Disclaimer and Privacy > Data Sharing, Privacy and EULA. Look for: “Agree to Enhanced Viewing Service.” Untick it. Then check: Settings > System > Advanced Settings > Enhanced Viewing Settings. Turn off the available ACR-related options. Also review Personalised Ads and Personalised Recommendations. Menu names can vary across Hisense models, operating systems and regions. > What should you take away from this? Your Smart TV isn’t just a screen anymore. story-ef7e8844fd3239056a9eed85.content:
For much of last year, about 2,500 US service members from the 15th Marine Expeditionary Unit sailed aboard three ships throughout the Pacific, conducting training exercises in the waters off South Korea, the Philippines, India, and Indonesia. At the same time, onboard the ships, an experiment was unfolding: The Marines in the unit responsible for sorting through foreign intelligence and making their superiors aware of possible local threats were for the first time using generative AI to do it, testing a leading AI tool the Pentagon has been funding.

Two officers tell us that they used the new system to help scour thousands of pieces of open-source intelligence—nonclassified articles, reports, images, videos—collected in the various countries where they operated, and that it did so far faster than was possible with the old method of analyzing them manually. Captain Kristin Enzenauer, for instance, says she used large language models to translate and summarize foreign news sources, while Captain Will Lowdon used AI to help write the daily and weekly intelligence reports he provided to his commanders. 

“We still need to validate the sources,” says Lowdon. But the unit’s commanders encouraged the use of large language models, he says, “because they provide a lot more efficiency during a dynamic situation.”

The generative AI tools they used were built by the defense-tech company Vannevar Labs, which in November was granted a production contract worth up to $99 million by the Pentagon’s startup-oriented Defense Innovation Unit with the goal of bringing its intelligence tech to more military units. The company, founded in 2019 by veterans of the CIA and US intelligence community, joins the likes of Palantir, Anduril, and Scale AI as a major beneficiary of the US military’s embrace of artificial intelligence—not only for physical technologies like drones and autonomous vehicles but also for software that is revolutionizing how the Pentagon collects, manages, and interprets data for warfare and surveillance. 

Though the US military has been developing computer vision models and similar AI tools, like those used in Project Maven, since 2017, the use of generative AI—tools that can engage in human-like conversation like those built by Vannevar Labs—represent a newer frontier.

The company applies existing large language models, including some from OpenAI and Microsoft, and some bespoke ones of its own to troves of open-source intelligence the company has been collecting since 2021. The scale at which this data is collected is hard to comprehend (and a large part of what sets Vannevar’s products apart): terabytes of data in 80 different languages are hoovered every day in 180 countries. The company says it is able to analyze social media profiles and breach firewalls in countries like China to get hard-to-access information; it also uses nonclassified data that is difficult to get online (gathered by human operatives on the ground), as well as reports from physical sensors that covertly monitor radio waves to detect illegal shipping activities. 

Vannevar then builds AI models to translate information, detect threats, and analyze political sentiment, with the results delivered through a chatbot interface that’s not unlike ChatGPT. The aim is to provide customers with critical information on topics as varied as international fentanyl supply chains and China’s efforts to secure rare earth minerals in the Philippines. 

“Our real focus as a company,” says Scott Philips, Vannevar Labs’ chief technology officer, is to “collect data, make sense of that data, and help the US make good decisions.” 

That approach is particularly appealing to the US intelligence apparatus because for years the world has been awash in more data than human analysts can possibly interpret—a problem that contributed to the 2003 founding of Palantir, a company with a market value of over $200 billion and known for its powerful and controversial tools, including a database that helps Immigration and Customs Enforcement search for and track information on undocumented immigrants. 

In 2019, Vannevar saw an opportunity to use large language models, which were then new on the scene, as a novel solution to the data conundrum. The technology could enable AI not just to collect data but to actually talk through an analysis with someone interactively.

Vannevar’s tools proved useful for the deployment in the Pacific, and Enzenauer and Lowdon say that while they were instructed to always double-check the AI’s work, they didn’t find inaccuracies to be a significant issue. Enzenauer regularly used the tool to track any foreign news reports in which the unit’s exercises were mentioned and to perform sentiment analysis, detecting the emotions and opinions expressed in text. Judging whether a foreign news article reflects a threatening or friendly opinion toward the unit is a task that on previous deployments she had to do manually.

“It was mostly by hand—researching, translating, coding, and analyzing the data,” she says. “It was definitely way more time-consuming than it was when using the AI.” 

Still, Enzenauer and Lowdon say there were hiccups, some of which would affect most digital tools: The ships had spotty internet connections much of the time, limiting how quickly the AI model could synthesize foreign intelligence, especially if it involved photos or video. 

With this first test completed, the unit’s commanding officer, Colonel Sean Dynan, said on a call with reporters in February that heavier use of generative AI was coming; this experiment was “the tip of the iceberg.” 

This is indeed the direction that the entire US military is barreling toward at full speed. In December, the Pentagon said it will spend $100 million in the next two years on pilots specifically for generative AI applications. In addition to Vannevar, it’s also turning to Microsoft and Palantir, which are working together on AI models that would make use of classified data. (The US is of course not alone in this approach; notably, Israel has been using AI to sort through information and even generate lists of targets in its war in Gaza, a practice that has been widely criticized.)

Perhaps unsurprisingly, plenty of people outside the Pentagon are warning about the potential risks of this plan, including Heidy Khlaaf, who is chief AI scientist at the AI Now Institute, a research organization, and has expertise in leading safety audits for AI-powered systems. She says this rush to incorporate generative AI into military decision-making ignores more foundational flaws of the technology: “We’re already aware of how LLMs are highly inaccurate, especially in the context of safety-critical applications that require precision.” 

Khlaaf adds that even if humans are “double-checking” the work of AI, there’s little reason to think they’re capable of catching every mistake. “‘Human-in-the-loop’ is not always a meaningful mitigation,” she says. When an AI model relies on thousands of data points to come to conclusions, “it wouldn’t really be possible for a human to sift through that amount of information to determine if the AI output was erroneous.”

One particular use case that concerns her is sentiment analysis, which she argues is “a highly subjective metric that even humans would struggle to appropriately assess based on media alone.” 

If AI perceives hostility toward US forces where a human analyst would not—or if the system misses hostility that is really there—the military could make an misinformed decision or escalate a situation unnecessarily.

Sentiment analysis is indeed a task that AI has not perfected. Philips, the Vannevar CTO, says the company has built models specifically to judge whether an article is pro-US or not, but MIT Technology Review was not able to evaluate them. 

Chris Mouton, a senior engineer for RAND, recently tested how well-suited generative AI is for the task. He evaluated leading models, including OpenAI’s GPT-4 and an older version of GPT fine-tuned to do such intelligence work, on how accurately they flagged foreign content as propaganda compared with human experts. “It’s hard,” he says, noting that AI struggled to identify more subtle types of propaganda. But he adds that the models could still be useful in lots of other analysis tasks. 

Another limitation of Vannevar’s approach, Khlaaf says, is that the usefulness of open-source intelligence is debatable. Mouton says that open-source data can be “pretty extraordinary,” but Khlaaf points out that unlike classified intel gathered through reconnaissance or wiretaps, it is exposed to the open internet—making it far more susceptible to misinformation campaigns, bot networks, and deliberate manipulation, as the US Army has warned.

For Mouton, the biggest open question now is whether these generative AI technologies will be simply one investigatory tool among many that analysts use—or whether they’ll produce the subjective analysis that’s relied upon and trusted in decision-making. “This is the central debate,” he says. 

What everyone agrees is that AI models are accessible—you can just ask them a question about complex pieces of intelligence, and they’ll respond in plain language. But it’s still in dispute what imperfections will be acceptable in the name of efficiency. 

Update: This story was updated to include additional context from Heidy Khlaaf.

تقريبًا نص السوق، وكثير من الجهات، خصوصًا المتوسطة والصغيرة، ما تقدر تبني مركز عمليات أمنية خاص فيها. فالطلب على مراقبة وكشف واستجابة تُدار من طرف ثاني بيكبر مع كل جهة جديدة تدخل السوق. ثانيًا أمن الأنظمة الصناعية OT. المشاريع الكبرى في الطاقة والمياه والصناعة والموانئ كلها تعتمد على أنظمة تحكم صناعي، وحماية هالأنظمة تحتاج خبرة مختلفة عن أمن تقنية المعلومات العادي. وهذا مجال المتخصصين فيه لسا قليل مقارنة بحجم الاحتياج، وهذي ملاحظة من عملي في هذا المجال، ما عندي لها رقم من تقرير. ثالثًا الامتثال والحوكمة. الهيئة نشرت قبل أيام جدول تصنيف مخالفات الأمن السيبراني وما يقابلها من العقوبات، وهو يحدد عقوبات تتدرج حسب حجم الجهة وتكرار المخالفة. هذا يرفع أهمية الامتثال عند الجهات، وأتوقع إنه يزيد الطلب على خدمات التقييم والتدقيق والاستشارات. وهذا استنتاج مني، وما فيه أرقام تثبته لحد الحين. رابعًا الأمن السحابي، لأن الجهات تنقل أنظمتها للبنية السحابية بشكل بسرعة، وكل نقلة تحتاج ضوابط جديدة. خامسًا الكفاءات. 22 ألف متخصص رقم كبير مقارنة بالسنوات الماضية، لكن حجم المشاريع القادمة يحتاج أكثر، وهذا يفتح الباب لشركات التدريب والتوظيف المتخصصة. اللي يقول السوق متشبع غالبًا يقصد إن المنافسة على العملاء الكبار صعبة، وهذا صحيح. لكن السوق يكبر والتنظيم واضح، والمشاريع اللي جاية كلها تحتاج حماية من أول يوم. لو أنت مستثمر أو صاحب فكرة، ابدأ من احتياج حقيقي عند جهة محددة.

story-f0b1f15ba7df9a4e123c041d.content: A viral X post asking whether your TV can secretly talk to your phone with inaudible sound hit 527K views today. Here's what you need to know. DK (@buildwithdk) posted on Nov 13, 2026 at 2:00 PM: "Your TV can secretly talk to your phone using sounds you can't hear. @grok is this true?" The post has about 3.3K likes, 904 reposts and 1.3K bookmarks. Grok answered yes. It said TVs, through ads or content, can emit near-ultrasonic beacons at around 18 to 20 kHz, which most humans can't hear. Phone microphones can pick them up. Apps then log the signal for cross-device ad tracking, linking what you watched to your phone profile. The technique is called ultrasonic cross-device tracking, or uXDT. Ad networks embed beacons in the audio tracks of TV ads. When a phone app recognizes the sound, it links that phone to the TV, the ad, and any other device that heard it. It only works if an app has microphone permission. There is a separate issue with smart TVs. They use automatic content recognition, or ACR. Samsung says ACR identifies content with audio fingerprinting through the TV's internal audio processor, not a speaker. A study found an LG TV contacting the analytics company Alphonso. Researchers have also alleged that unclear sounds and unmatched wake-word interactions could be stored locally. The claim is disputed. One reply says David Pogue told CBS News "Sunday Morning" there was zero communication between phone and TV ads. Pogue's CBS segment looked at why targeted ads can seem weirdly specific. Key numbers: - 527K views on the original post - About 3.3K likes, 904 reposts, 1.3K bookmarks - 18 to 20 kHz, the near-ultrasonic range Grok cited - Requires phone microphone permission for an app Replies show people are worried about TV and phone privacy, especially Samsung and LG sets, and some say they've unplugged their TVs.

الاستخدام (تصريح/تلميح): تصريح صريح وتلميح هيكلي حول استخدام هندسة البرمجيات لتطوير منظومات صواريخ موجهة وطائرات ومقذوفات متقدمة. التفاصيل التشغيلية: استخدام Claude Code كبديل لمهندسي البرمجيات البشرية لتطوير برمجيات التوجيه والملاحة والتحكم (GNC)، دمج الطيار الآلي مفتوح المصدر على حواسيب طيران بحجم الهاتف، كتابة خوارزميات التثبيت، وإجراء محاكاة للطيران واختبارات حية ميدانية. بيانات المرجع: رقم الصفحة: صفحة 112. رقم السطر / الموقع: قسم GTG-87001 (Summary). بداية الفقرة: "We identified a cell of threat actors based in northern Yemen..." نهاية الفقرة: "...with a stated range goal above 2,000 km;" 2. الاستطلاع البحري وتطوير أدوات الاستخبارات والتوجيه (GTG-30005) الجهة أو الوكيل: جهة تهديد ترتبط بمرجعية إيران (Iran-nexus threat actor). طبيعة الاستخدام (تصريح/تلميح): تصريح صريح بشأن استخدام الذكاء الاصطناعي لجمع وتحليل البيانات المتاحة للجمهور لتطوير توصيات استهداف للقوات البحرية الأمريكية في المنطقة، وتصميم برمجيات لأنظمة المراقبة المحلية. التفاصيل التشغيلية: تجميع كتيبات استهداف، كشط قوائم الأفراد العسكريين من الصور العامة، تحليل معرفات السفن والطائرات، وكتابة أبحاث الثغرات الأمنية في محطات الاتصالات البحرية ومعدات الشركات المصنعة، بالإضافة إلى دمج التعرف على لوحات السيارات مع اعتراض معرفات الأجهزة المحمولة. بيانات المرجع: رقم الصفحة: صفحة 106. رقم السطر / الموقع: قسم GTG-30005 (Naval reconnaissance). بداية الفقرة: "In another investigation, we identified and disrupted an Iran-nexus threat actor..." نهاية الفقرة: "...and industrial control products." 3. العمليات الاستخباراتيّة وتحليل شبكات التواصل الاجتماعي (GTG-34007 و GTG-54009) الجهة أو الوكيل: وحدات إيرانية وكيانات تجارية مرتبطة (مثل S2T Unlocking Cyberspace كبائع استخبارات تجاري، ووحدات تابعة للحرس الثوري والأجهزة الأمنية الداخلية الإيرانية). طبيعة الاستخدام (تصريح/تلميح): تصريح صريح في استهداف مستخدمي وسائل التواصل الاجتماعي في إيران ومنطقة الخليج العربي لبناء منصات مراقبة وتصنيف السكان. التفاصيل التشغيلية: استخدام الذكاء الاصطناعي لتحليل، تصنيف، وبناء ملفات تعريفية لأنشطة وسائل التواصل الاجتماعي، وتطوير ملخصات استخباراتية باللغة العربية، بالإضافة إلى تطوير ملحق متصفح خبيث (Firefox extension) لحصد هويات المستخدمين. بيانات المرجع: رقم الصفحة: صفحة 82 (وتفاصيلGTG-34007 في صفحة 101-102). رقم السطر / الموقع: الفقرة الأولى من قسم GTG-54009. بداية الفقرة: "In June 2026, we banned an account that used Claude..." نهاية الفقرة: "...is an Israeli-Singaporean commercial intelligence vendor."
